document.title: 9.3 – Career & Technical Education (CTE) Content Area: 21st Century Life and Careers

649F073351BC480AA2275AF42D97729D.description:
Model how the properties of water can change as water
moves through the water cycle.

937F8C3B0F414C029E672A6E0150A9D2.description:
Trace a path a drop of water might follow through the
water cycle.

A4107A4699A041DBA4F8510F5B6120F7.description:
Observe daily cloud patterns, types of precipitation, and
temperature, and categorize the clouds by the conditions
that form precipitation.

4CA162546E02483F9B3A672A7206A273.description:
Biogeochemical Cycles : The biogeochemical cycles in the Earth systems include the flow of
microscopic and macroscopic resources from one reservoir in the hydrosphere, geosphere,
atmosphere, or biosphere to another, are driven by Earth's internal and external sources of energy,
and are impacted by human activity.

150DEEF3E1A14C06AAFC84C40A9D9F8A.description:
Identify patterns in data collected from basic weather
instruments.

D663584C258042DFBE973CADF74A5B15.description:
Climate and Weather : Earth’s weather and climate systems are the result of complex
interactions between land, ocean, ice, and atmosphere.

661D2329EB944657B854C5B1B9ADBE58.description:
Develop a general set of rules to predict temperature
changes of Earth materials, such as water, soil, and sand,
when placed in the Sun and in the shade.

D2888A7497B348E89DE69F0A33176A4A.description: Energy in Earth Systems : Internal and external sources of energy drive Earth systems.

E004E961B4084BC894D4C9189C75A9D3.description: Categorize unknown samples as either rocks or minerals

A3439FC3C0C548BAA74181F54C67D9F6.description: Create a model to represent how soil is formed.

1B7E7EEDC0454EA7A3E2DA7873E6B3B7.description:
Properties of Earth Materials : Earth’s composition is unique, is related to the origin of our
solar system, and provides us with the raw resources needed to sustain life.

40A0C78A1A3245369087748AD381D344.description:
Use data gathered from observations of fossils to argue
whether a given fossil is terrestrial or marine in origin.

C8718C67013240DB98529C3D8D7C8A5D.description:
History of Earth : From the time that Earth formed from a nebula 4.6 billion years ago, it has
been evolving as a result of geologic, biological, physical, and chemical processes.

872C13941AA34E15889EE1D809FC97BC.description:
Analyze and evaluate evidence in the form of data tables and photographs to categorize and relate solar system
objects (e.g., planets, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids,
and comets).

AA1CF25B76B949BE9181C9A2171DD61C.description:
Generate a model with explanatory value that explains
both why objects roll down ramps as well as why the
Moon orbits Earth.

17C30215200D4FC1ADD079B4DCB958D7.description:
Identify patterns of the Moon’s appearance and make
predictions about its future appearance based
observational data.

E99B682A292F4BE884BF04F7FE019B7B.description:
Formulate a general description of the daily motion of the
Sun across the sky based on shadow observations.
Explain how shadows could be used to tell the time of
day.

F8290EC01CD7485BA81246B9C06B42D9.description:
Objects in the Universe : Our universe has been expanding and evolving for 13.7 billion years
under the influence of gravitational and nuclear forces. As gravity governs its expansion,
organizational patterns, and the movement of celestial bodies, nuclear forces within stars govern its
evolution through the processes of stellar birth and death. These same processes governed the
formation of our solar system 4.6 billion years ago.

B55F8F4E049145ECA1F02217D693C47D.description:
Earth Systems Science: All students will understand that Earth operates as a set of complex,
dynamic, and interconnected systems, and is a part of the all-encompassing system of the universe.

8E7FB32E826D4E128652DDD97C5C1010.description:
Evaluate similar populations in an ecosystem with regard
to their ability to thrive and grow.

796F1F323B4F4B3095EE84EB4EA31258.description:
Model an adaptation to a species that would increase its
chances of survival, should the environment become
wetter, dryer, warmer, or colder over time.

919F6E64C33A4C58BE23893D54C443FF.description:
Evolution and Diversity: : Sometimes, differences between organisms of the same kind
provide advantages for surviving and reproducing in different environments. These selective
differences may lead to dramatic changes in characteristics of organisms in a population over
extremely long periods of time.

624AB1CA2B164E9E9971672A42B4CB8D.description:
Compare the physical characteristics of the different
stages of the life cycle of an individual organism, and
compare the characteristics of life stages among species.

BFFFB27456B740128A22DBA9063216E3.description:
Heredity and Reproduction : Organisms reproduce, develop, and have predictable life cycles.
Organisms contain genetic information that influences their traits, and they pass this on to their
offspring during reproduction.

8C3CC9DD73ED4F569236765194ED615C.description:
Explain the consequences of rapid ecosystem change (e.g., flooding, wind storms, snowfall, volcanic eruptions),
and compare them to consequences of gradual ecosystem
change (e.g., gradual increase or decrease in daily
temperatures, change in yearly rainfall).

F26F9319ED2C45749BFCEF43AACAC9AA.description:
Predict the biotic and abiotic characteristics of an
unfamiliar organism’s habitat.

8E8269212F7A4930ACD6EFC0B82B104E.description:
Interdependence : All animals and most plants depend on both other organisms and their
environment to meet their basic needs.

74E32BC13E8F40DCBC206426EA7D9913.description:
Identify sources of energy (food) in a variety of settings
(farm, zoo, ocean, forest).

28EAFDB60DBF41EBAB3005DCA977E728.description:
Matter and Energy Transformations : Food is required for energy and building cellular
materials. Organisms in an ecosystem have different ways of obtaining food, and some organisms
obtain their food directly from other organisms.

787AB243BABC46D99F4D73976D965CC1.description:
Describe the interactions of systems involved in carrying
out everyday life activities.

F75CEE2FC2274EBB83A3D3ACA8A25028.description:
Compare and contrast structures that have similar
functions in various organisms, and explain how those
functions may be carried out by structures that have
different physical appearances.

7471A2E069D245EC909DD26C41E22F6F.description: Develop and use evidence-based criteria to determine if an unfamiliar object is living or nonliving.

4C2E527305404807AB2CEA22C07184FE.description:
Organization and Development : Living organisms are composed of cellular units (structures)
that carry out functions required for life. Cellular units are composed of molecules, which also carry
out biological functions.

08B03E4BCCED4875B8AB23C5DC8E5F67.description:
Life Science: All students will understand that life science principles are powerful conceptual
tools for making sense of the complexity, diversity, and interconnectedness of life on Earth. Order in
natural systems arises in accordance with rules that govern the physical world, and the order of
natural systems can be modeled and predicted through the use of mathematics.

B2AD3437A6CB4031914910BBDAFA82CE.description:
Investigate, construct, and generalize rules for the effect
that force of gravity has on balls of different sizes and
weights.

20EE23ECB3BB433ABE3261D0D019C21F.description:
Investigate and categorize materials based on their
interaction with magnets.

15C7E82231F04E77A684BE0C5435A78E.description: Identify the force that starts something moving or changes its speed or direction of motion.

146ADC2C190C478398421948ABA2F6F4.description:
Demonstrate through modeling that motion is a change in
position over a period of time.

266A73614101498B8A4F6D534F4042CD.description:
Forces and Motion : It takes energy to change the motion of objects. The energy change is
understood in terms of forces.

BF9B926AEC954DDCA795C79F11A6104E.description:
Repair an electric circuit by completing a closed loop that
includes wires, a battery (or batteries), and at least one
other electrical component to produce observable change.

B97B8907B9E841CEABC9A0D36A6AAEE7.description:
Energy Transfer and Conservation : The conservation of energy can be demonstrated by
keeping track of familiar forms of energy as they are transferred from one object to another.

1334D580695547C9B135736E87ABB81E.description:
Illustrate and explain what happens when light travels
from air into water.

8002DD9E895143E49A82FEF6285FDED3.description:
Draw and label diagrams showing several ways that
energy can be transferred from one place to another.

B62ED0930F14439481C494FF39348072.description:
Compare the flow of heat through metals and nonmetals
by taking and analyzing measurements.

EE9550B559ED47CA94BEA3EF17BCCAC1.description:
Compare various forms of energy as observed in everyday
life and describe their applications.

A0445194A82944EA9EBCC5374D542215.description:
Forms of Energy : Knowing the characteristics of familiar forms of energy, including potential
and kinetic energy, is useful in coming to the understanding that, for the most part, the natural
world can be explained and is predictable.

6C5B8A2CD8574AEBAABBCC2FC7956C92.description:
Predict and explain what happens when a common
substance, such as shortening or candle wax, is heated to
melting and then cooled to a solid.

C8A413A9D84E44098C33FCF3E610CBC0.description:
Changes in Matter : Substances can undergo physical or chemical changes to form new
substances. Each change involves energy.

F3C40B2A640045219ED8F7398684757B.description:
Categorize objects based on the ability to absorb or reflect
light and conduct heat or electricity.

CD6D843BD1A747D8A9A2819DFB25FB2E.description:
Determine the weight and volume of common objects
using appropriate tools.

E73157BB97BD4D5195CFA0308F2A1EBB.description:
Plan and carry out an investigation to distinguish among
solids, liquids, and gasses.

54D556CE32CD4D4898C1BAF55875F785.description:
Identify objects that are composed of a single substance
and those that are composed of more than one substance
using simple tools found in the classroom.

8ACE019D82B449E6949D8F4BC761F0D0.description:
Properties of Matter : All objects and substances in the natural world are composed of matter.
Matter has two fundamental properties: matter takes up space, and matter has inertia.

B46F9A2A9F204876BA10A8C5315ADDFE.description:
Physical Science: All students will understand that physical science principles, including
fundamental ideas about matter, energy, and motion, are powerful conceptual tools for making
sense of phenomena in physical, living, and Earth systems science.

A5331CBBAB3B4C4C85C6E2C8F5434532.description:
Handle and treat organisms humanely, responsibly, and
ethically.

AD352C6CF7B64C8B96194A27BC452344.description:
Demonstrate how to safely use tools, instruments, and
supplies.

51F399F3CB7145978465EA52552321C6.description:
Work collaboratively to pose, refine, and evaluate
questions, investigations, models, and theories.

1396920F92784AE18AE894A99D44A493.description:
Actively participate in discussions about student data,
questions, and understandings.

D28ECE89961E4CCB973C71E6B0A6A322.description:
Participate Productively in Science : The growth of scientific knowledge involves critique and
communication, which are social practices that are governed by a core set of values and norms.

27013E7D848040E28AF654DC58216CE2.description:
Present evidence to interpret and/or predict cause-andeffect
outcomes of investigations.

4FFCD52CD3614EC39F5D9919A627820B.description:
Revise predictions or explanations on the basis of learning
new information.

09E34F2B97B5484481EB5AAED8598699.description:
Monitor and reflect on one’s own knowledge regarding
how ideas change over time.

AB1983E72DE5485EAF5DC1424E78FD8E.description: Reflect on Scientific Knowledge : Scientific knowledge builds on itself over time.

FB5CCD40A4A84425B79F8C4830D17A7E.description:
Communicate and justify explanations with reasonable
and logical arguments.

F1D651E170FC4027AF03FD36AE4C94D9.description:
Measure, gather, evaluate, and share evidence using tools
and technologies.

88FDE0B790A34A7594A5826D78511CBA.description:
Design and follow simple plans using systematic
observations to explore questions and predictions.

115D3B0E801F457F8020B02AC5319F9A.description:
Generate Scientific Evidence Through Active Investigations : Students master the
conceptual, mathematical, physical, and computational tools that need to be applied when
constructing and evaluating claims.

5AAA394E73FB4E458332E9CE53DB56B1.description:
Use scientific facts, measurements, observations, and
patterns in nature to build and critique scientific
arguments.

921F0910A9804E99A0E7ED6EB31426A2.description:
Use outcomes of investigations to build and refine
questions, models, and explanations.

B6D7F74F67E0421AAD739C9CCB5A38FA.description:
Demonstrate understanding of the interrelationships
among fundamental concepts in the physical, life, and
Earth systems sciences.

A74B6C81C52E4238BA2977F76CBDADEE.description:
Understand Scientific Explanations : Students understand core concepts and principles of
science and use measurement and observation tools to assist in categorizing, representing, and
interpreting the natural and designed world.

7B4B34E9F43946AFA82F5C4D992CBC95.description:
Science Practices: All students will understand that science is both a body of knowledge and
an evidence-based, model-building enterprise that continually extends, refines, and revises
knowledge. The four Science Practices strands encompass the knowledge and reasoning skills that
students must acquire to be proficient in science.

FAC039AA1DEC49CA809452E0F1870107.description:
Demonstrate emergent awareness for conservation,
recycling, and respect for the environment (e.g., turning
off water faucets, using paper from a classroom scrap box
when whole sheets are not needed, keeping the
playground neat and clean).

FA01716681C14B1686EF69699DD66307.description:
Biogeochemical Cycles : The biogeochemical cycles in the Earth systems include the flow of
microscopic and macroscopic resources from one reservoir in the hydrosphere, geosphere,
atmosphere, or biosphere to another, are driven by Earth's internal and external sources of energy,
and are impacted by human activity.

7677B7F470E44D6D93F5097DE7CFFD4D.description:
Climate and Weather : Earth’s weather and climate systems are the result of complex
interactions between land, ocean, ice, and atmosphere.

87DEA52D62C249F6B957EC0C88784D59.description:
Explore the effects of sunlight on living and nonliving
things.

1647A3657AF54B7AA37790F5D4177705.description: Energy in Earth Systems : Internal and external sources of energy drive Earth systems.

DECD3EB810814D48B163C68867BC1BFD.description:
Explore and describe characteristics of and concepts about
soil, rocks, water, and air.

FD7C75AE06B24A23B7AAAB33BB7357FF.description:
Properties of Earth Materials : Earth’s composition is unique, is related to the origin of our
solar system, and provides us with the raw resources needed to sustain life.

5BF1C54A46B54F449C4164A67E29EAE9.description:
Earth Systems Science: All students will understand that Earth operates as a set of complex,
dynamic, and interconnected systems, and is a part of the all-encompassing system of the universe.

AA130ADC072D4D6CB7723F3FB5300E85.description:
Observe and record change over time and cycles of
change that affect living things (e.g., use baby
photographs to discuss human change and growth,
observe and photograph tree growth and leaf changes
throughout the year, monitor the life cycle of a plant).

75095C098DBD4156AA14A1712750E4F0.description:
Heredity and Reproduction : Organisms reproduce, develop, and have predictable life cycles.
Organisms contain genetic information that influences their traits, and they pass this on to their
offspring during reproduction.

167B54B71E5B4BF5BD8469E8EBF4A2D6.description:
Observe and describe how natural habitats provide for the
basic needs of plants and animals with respect to shelter,
food, water, air, and light (e.g., dig outside in the soil to
investigate the kinds of animal life that live in and around
the ground).

053AA31D96B4496B8092E5191E6200DC.description:
Interdependence : All animals and most plants depend on both other organisms and their
environment to meet their basic needs.

D95E6AE01A074890ABBF8D8AA49C6F3E.description:
Observe and describe how plants and animals obtain food
from their environment, such as by observing the
interactions between organisms in a natural habitat.

E2D6B7B7985743FB8FE6D4DF1032266A.description:
Matter and Energy Transformations : Food is required for energy and building cellular
materials. Organisms in an ecosystem have different ways of obtaining food, and some organisms
obtain their food directly from other organisms

EF5853338A3C4BF585A6B8C1F3587ED0.description:
Investigate and compare the basic physical characteristics
of plants, humans, and other animals.

6ED20795D2684C109694C88AE7A66756.description:
Investigate and compare the basic physical characteristics
of plants, humans, and other animals.

C8287C7BF3984027AC82394DD3AE53CF.description:
A. Organization and Development : Living organisms are composed of cellular units (structures)
that carry out functions required for life. Cellular units are composed of molecules, which also carry
out biological functions.

52A5954054F748AAB50E74F1C263DCA6.description:
Life Science: All students will understand that life science principles are powerful conceptual
tools for making sense of the complexity, diversity, and interconnectedness of life on Earth. Order in
natural systems arises in accordance with rules that govern the physical world, and the order of
natural systems can be modeled and predicted through the use of mathematics.

10FBD7A62C2F42B2ACA6A2D42837BCDA.description:
Investigate how and why things move (e.g., slide blocks,
balance structures, push structures over, use ramps to
explore how far and how fast different objects move or
roll).

88CBDE6270284F548008C52390ADE553.description:
Forces and Motion : It takes energy to change the motion of objects. The energy change is
understood in terms of forces.

692CD565B66F4A26B34AD0026F920C20.description:
Predict and confirm the brightness of a light, the volume
of sound, or the amount of heat when given the number
of batteries, or the size of batteries.

5329225255A945D1AC5B3EE091843688.description:
Energy Transfer and Conservation : The conservation of energy can be demonstrated by
keeping track of familiar forms of energy as they are transferred from one object to another.

4FDCAF8375FF48AD83134A1996269749.description:
Investigate sound, heat, and light energy (e.g., the pitch
and volume of sound made by commercially made and
homemade instruments, looking for shadows on the
playground over time and under different weather
conditions) through one or more of the senses.

B8B3AA961D9D4F58862605EA576B7E04.description:
Forms of Energy : Knowing the characteristics of familiar forms of energy, including potential
and kinetic energy, is useful in coming to the understanding that, for the most part, the natural
world can be explained and is predictable.

B6F83F166BB349D3AF53FC297DF3572C.description:
Explore changes in liquids and solids when substances are
combined, heated, or cooled (e.g., mix sand or clay with
various amounts of water; mix different colors of tempera
paints; freeze and melt water and other liquids).

F2FD63B71AD04907AA8972B55EA62D25.description:
Changes in Matter : Substances can undergo physical or chemical changes to form new
substances. Each change involves energy.

D4C00CE3CFD048D8AD81C6DFBFF5AA86.description:
Observe, manipulate, sort, and describe objects and
materials (e.g., water, sand, clay, paint, glue, various
types of blocks, collections of objects, simple household
items that can be taken apart, or objects made of wood,
metal, or cloth) in the classroom and outdoor environment
based on size, shape, color, texture, and weight.

24F1AC3C3E574C46B530397434E1D999.description:
Properties of Matter : All objects and substances in the natural world are composed of matter.
Matter has two fundamental properties: matter takes up space, and matter has inertia.

76BF205A982E4E9C9908CF31CA96042C.description:
Physical Science: All students will understand that physical science principles, including
fundamental ideas about matter, energy, and motion, are powerful conceptual tools for making
sense of phenomena in physical, living, and Earth systems science.

5DF22BE42F4346F2BF8659187DF4F70E.description:
Represent observations and work through drawing,
recording data, and “writing.”

C17D3C5FD1A14787A93575A9996DA9F3.description:
Participate Productively in Science : The growth of scientific knowledge involves critique and
communication, which are social practices that are governed by a core set of values and norms.

56F45C8FF6BC4EC4BA6AD43BE2D01EE3.description:
Communicate with other children and adults to share
observations, pursue questions, and make predictions
and/or conclusions.

5A5D306CEB2B42CB8C683F19B285F94A.description: Reflect on Scientific Knowledge : Scientific knowledge builds on itself over time.

19B7BF0A036647E884EE7672AF4DBEB2.description:
Identify and use basic tools and technology to extend
exploration in conjunction with science investigations.

335F04EBF6EE48159998D8478D2DA2F4.description:
Use basic science terms and topic-related science
vocabulary.

06F56E2576F945419D3B128D1E50AC9B.description:
Observe, question, predict, and investigate materials,
objects, and phenomena (e.g., using simple tools to crack
a nut and look inside) during indoor and outdoor
classroom activities and during any longer-term
investigations.

1437C90011FA424D8A40F3092A719ECD.description:
Generate Scientific Evidence Through Active Investigations : Students master the
conceptual, mathematical, physical, and computational tools that need to be applied when
constructing and evaluating claims.

E1E415CB3D774A27A1B9CBEECCC10428.description:
Display curiosity about science objects, materials,
activities, and longer-term investigations in progress.

068AFCBFFC0C436DB861BB124B67654C.description:
Understand Scientific Explanations : Students understand core concepts and principles of
science and use measurement and observation tools to assist in categorizing, representing, and
interpreting the natural and designed world.

E62D35A11FAA4FF49B504BC08A9F7065.description:
Science Practices: All students will understand that science is both a body of knowledge and
an evidence-based, model-building enterprise that continually extends, refines, and revises
knowledge. The four Science Practices strands encompass the knowledge and reasoning skills that
students must acquire to be proficient in science.

document.title: New Jersey Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

BD917F30DFE601317A0C68A86D17958E.description: Describe qualitatively the functional relationship between two quantities by analyzing a graph (e.g., where the function is increasing or decreasing, linear or nonlinear). Sketch a graph that exhibits the qualitative features of a function that has been described verbally.

BD911F60DFE601317A0B68A86D17958E.description: Construct a function to model a linear relationship between two quantities. Determine the rate of change and initial value of the function from a description of a relationship or from two (x, y) values, including reading these from a table or from a graph. Interpret the rate of change and initial value of a linear function in terms of the situation it models, and in terms of its graph or a table of values.

BD90D180DFE601317A0A68A86D17958E.description: Use functions to model relationships between quantities.

BD908420DFE601317A0968A86D17958E.description: Interpret the equation y = mx + b as defining a linear function, whose graph is a straight line; give examples of functions that are not linear.
comments: For example, the function A = s² giving the area of a square as a function of its side length is not linear because its graph contains the points (1,1), (2,4) and (3,9), which are not on a straight line.

BD9040B0DFE601317A0868A86D17958E.description: Compare properties of two functions each represented in a different way (algebraically, graphically, numerically in tables, or by verbal descriptions).
comments: For example, given a linear function represented by a table of values and a linear function represented by an algebraic expression, determine which function has the greater rate of change.

BD8FF6C0DFE601317A0768A86D17958E.description: Understand that a function is a rule that assigns to each input exactly one output. The graph of a function is the set of ordered pairs consisting of an input and the corresponding output.
comments: Function notation is not required in Grade 8.

BD8F19A0DFE601317A0468A86D17958E.description: Understand that patterns of association can also be seen in bivariate categorical data by displaying frequencies and relative frequencies in a two-way table. Construct and interpret a two-way table summarizing data on two categorical variables collected from the same subjects. Use relative frequencies calculated for rows or columns to describe possible association between the two variables.
comments: For example, collect data from students in your class on whether or not they have a curfew on school nights and whether or not they have assigned chores at home. Is there evidence that those who have a curfew also tend to have chores?

BD8ED620DFE601317A0368A86D17958E.description: Use the equation of a linear model to solve problems in the context of bivariate measurement data, interpreting the slope and intercept.
comments: For example, in a linear model for a biology experiment, interpret a slope of 1.5 cm/hr as meaning that an additional hour of sunlight each day is associated with an additional 1.5 cm in mature plant height.

BD8E9290DFE601317A0268A86D17958E.description: Know that straight lines are widely used to model relationships between two quantitative variables. For scatter plots that suggest a linear association, informally fit a straight line, and informally assess the model fit by judging the closeness of the data points to the line.

BD8E4290DFE601317A0168A86D17958E.description: Construct and interpret scatter plots for bivariate measurement data to investigate patterns of association between two quantities. Describe patterns such as clustering, outliers, positive or negative association, linear association, and nonlinear association.

BD8DF1B0DFE601317A0068A86D17958E.description: Investigate patterns of association in bivariate data.

BD8D49D0DFE6013179FE68A86D17958E.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems leading to two linear equations in two variables.
comments: For example, given coordinates for two pairs of points, determine whether the line through the first pair of points intersects the line through the second pair.
For example, 3x + 2y = 5 and 3x + 2y = 6 have no solution because 3x + 2y cannot simultaneously be 5 and 6.
BD8D0540DFE6013179FD68A86D17958E.description: Solve systems of two linear equations in two variables algebraically, and estimate solutions by graphing the equations. Solve simple cases by inspection.

BD8CC0D0DFE6013179FC68A86D17958E.description: Understand that solutions to a system of two linear equations in two variables correspond to points of intersection of their graphs, because points of intersection satisfy both equations simultaneously.

BD8C7BC0DFE6013179FB68A86D17958E.description: Analyze and solve pairs of simultaneous linear equations.

BD8C3280DFE6013179FA68A86D17958E.description: Solve linear equations with rational number coefficients, including equations whose solutions require expanding expressions using the distributive property and collecting like terms.

BD8BD670DFE6013179F968A86D17958E.description: Give examples of linear equations in one variable with one solution, infinitely many solutions, or no solutions. Show which of these possibilities is the case by successively transforming the given equation into simpler forms, until an equivalent equation of the form x = a, a = a, or a = b results (where a and b are different numbers).

BD8B79D0DFE6013179F868A86D17958E.description: Solve linear equations in one variable.

BD8B3650DFE6013179F768A86D17958E.description: Analyze and solve linear equations and pairs of simultaneous linear equations.

BD8AF0B0DFE6013179F668A86D17958E.description: Use similar triangles to explain why the slope m is the same between any two distinct points on a non-vertical line in the coordinate plane; derive the equation y = mx for a line through the origin and the equation y = mx + b for a line intercepting the vertical axis at b.

comments: For example, compare a distance-time graph to a distance-time equation to determine which of two moving objects has greater speed.
BD8AA910DFE6013179F568A86D17958E.description: Graph proportional relationships, interpreting the unit rate as the slope of the graph. Compare two different proportional relationships represented in different ways.

BD8A6150DFE6013179F468A86D17958E.description: Understand the connections between proportional relationships, lines, and linear equations.

BD8A1590DFE6013179F368A86D17958E.description: Perform operations with numbers expressed in scientific notation, including problems where both decimal and scientific notation are used. Use scientific notation and choose units of appropriate size for measurements of very large or very small quantities (e.g., use millimeters per year for seafloor spreading). Interpret scientific notation that has been generated by technology.

comments: For example, estimate the population of the United States as 3 × 10<sup>8</sup> and the population of the world as 7 × 10<sup>9</sup>, and determine that the world population is more than 20 times larger.
BD89C4A0DFE6013179F268A86D17958E.description: Use numbers expressed in the form of a single digit times an integer power of 10 to estimate very large or very small quantities, and to express how many times as much one is than the other.

BD897FD0DFE6013179F168A86D17958E.description: Use square root and cube root symbols to represent solutions to equations of the form x² = p and x³ = p, where p is a positive rational number. Evaluate square roots of small perfect squares and cube roots of small perfect cubes. Know that √2 is irrational.

BD893CA0DFE6013179F068A86D17958E.description: Know and apply the properties of integer exponents to generate equivalent numerical expressions.
comments: For example, 3² × 3<sup>-5</sup> = 3<sup>-3</sup> = 1/3³ = 1/27.

BD88F7E0DFE6013179EF68A86D17958E.description: Work with radicals and integer exponents.

BD885170DFE6013179ED68A86D17958E.description: Use rational approximations of irrational numbers to compare the size of irrational numbers, locate them approximately on a number line diagram, and estimate the value of expressions (e.g., π²).
comments: For example, by truncating the decimal expansion of √2, show that √2 is between 1 and 2, then between 1.4 and 1.5, and explain how to continue on to get better approximations.

BD87F960DFE6013179EC68A86D17958E.description: Know that numbers that are not rational are called irrational. Understand informally that every number has a decimal expansion; for rational numbers show that the decimal expansion repeats eventually, and convert a decimal expansion which repeats eventually into a rational number.

BD87A9D0DFE6013179EB68A86D17958E.description: Know that there are numbers that are not rational, and approximate them by rational numbers.

BD872340DFE6013179E968A86D17958E.description: Know the formulas for the volumes of cones, cylinders, and spheres and use them to solve real-world and mathematical problems.

BD86DD30DFE6013179E868A86D17958E.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving volume of cylinders, cones, and spheres.

BD8691D0DFE6013179E768A86D17958E.description: Apply the Pythagorean Theorem to find the distance between two points in a coordinate system.

BD862A90DFE6013179E668A86D17958E.description: Apply the Pythagorean Theorem to determine unknown side lengths in right triangles in real-world and mathematical problems in two and three dimensions.

BD85D8B0DFE6013179E568A86D17958E.description: Explain a proof of the Pythagorean Theorem and its converse.

BD8594D0DFE6013179E468A86D17958E.description: Understand and apply the Pythagorean Theorem.

comments: For example, arrange three copies of the same triangle so that the sum of the three angles appears to form a line, and give an argument in terms of transversals why this is so.
BD854720DFE6013179E368A86D17958E.description: Use informal arguments to establish facts about the angle sum and exterior angle of triangles, about the angles created when parallel lines are cut by a transversal, and the angle-angle criterion for similarity of triangles.

BD84F930DFE6013179E268A86D17958E.description: Understand that a two-dimensional figure is similar to another if the second can be obtained from the first by a sequence of rotations, reflections, translations, and dilations; given two similar two-dimensional figures, describe a sequence that exhibits the similarity between them.

BD84B1B0DFE6013179E168A86D17958E.description: Describe the effect of dilations, translations, rotations, and reflections on two-dimensional figures using coordinates.

BD8463D0DFE6013179E068A86D17958E.description: Understand that a two-dimensional figure is congruent to another if the second can be obtained from the first by a sequence of rotations, reflections, and translations; given two congruent figures, describe a sequence that exhibits the congruence between them.

BD840FB0DFE6013179DF68A86D17958E.description: Parallel lines are taken to parallel lines.

BD83BF70DFE6013179DE68A86D17958E.description: Angles are taken to angles of the same measure.

BD8352C0DFE6013179DD68A86D17958E.description: Lines are taken to lines, and line segments to line segments of the same length.

BD82F5F0DFE6013179DC68A86D17958E.description: Verify experimentally the properties of rotations, reflections, and translations:

BD8285A0DFE6013179DB68A86D17958E.description: Understand congruence and similarity using physical models, transparencies, or geometry software.

BD81DE00DFE6013179D968A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

BD818DF0DFE6013179D868A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.
BD8017E0DFE6013179D468A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

comments: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

BD7F6FC0DFE6013179D268A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: New Jersey Common Core State Standards for English Language Arts and Literacy

BF2D94A0DFE601317CFA68A86D17958E.description: Use words and phrases acquired through conversations, reading and being read to, and responding to texts, including using adjectives and adverbs to describe (e.g., When other kids are happy that makes me happy).

BF2D4690DFE601317CF968A86D17958E.description: Distinguish shades of meaning among closely related verbs (e.g., toss, throw, hurl) and closely related adjectives (e.g., thin, slender, skinny, scrawny).

BF2CFF10DFE601317CF868A86D17958E.description: Identify real-life connections between words and their use (e.g., describe foods that are spicy or juicy).

BF2CB710DFE601317CF768A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of word relationships and nuances in word meanings.

BF2C6D90DFE601317CF668A86D17958E.description: Use glossaries and beginning dictionaries, both print and digital, to determine or clarify the meaning of words and phrases.

BF2C1D10DFE601317CF568A86D17958E.description: Use knowledge of the meaning of individual words to predict the meaning of compound words (e.g., birdhouse, lighthouse, housefly; bookshelf, notebook, bookmark).

BF2BA660DFE601317CF468A86D17958E.description: Use a known root word as a clue to the meaning of an unknown word with the same root (e.g., addition, additional).

BF2B4570DFE601317CF368A86D17958E.description: Determine the meaning of the new word formed when a known prefix is added to a known word (e.g., happy/unhappy, tell/retell).

BF2AFC80DFE601317CF268A86D17958E.description: Use sentence-level context as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.

BF2AB3D0DFE601317CF168A86D17958E.description: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases based on grade 2 reading and content, choosing flexibly from an array of strategies.

BF2A1AC0DFE601317CEF68A86D17958E.description: Compare formal and informal uses of English.

BF29BBF0DFE601317CEE68A86D17958E.description: Use knowledge of language and its conventions when writing, speaking, reading, or listening.

BF291600DFE601317CEC68A86D17958E.description: Consult reference materials, including beginning dictionaries, as needed to check and correct spellings.

BF28BCD0DFE601317CEB68A86D17958E.description: Generalize learned spelling patterns when writing words (e.g., cage → badge; boy → boil).

BF286590DFE601317CEA68A86D17958E.description: Use an apostrophe to form contractions and frequently occurring possessives.

BF281A10DFE601317CE968A86D17958E.description: Use commas in greetings and closings of letters.

BF27C3D0DFE601317CE868A86D17958E.description: Capitalize holidays, product names, and geographic names.

BF277C50DFE601317CE768A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.

BF273560DFE601317CE668A86D17958E.description: Produce, expand, and rearrange complete simple and compound sentences (e.g., The boy watched the movie; The little boy watched the movie; The action movie was watched by the little boy).

BF26EDD0DFE601317CE568A86D17958E.description: Use adjectives and adverbs, and choose between them depending on what is to be modified.

BF26A430DFE601317CE468A86D17958E.description: Form and use the past tense of frequently occurring irregular verbs (e.g., sat, hid, told).

The determinant of a square matrix is nonzero if and only if the matrix has a multiplicative inverse.

comments: Modeling is best interpreted not as a collection of isolated topics but in relation to other standards. Making mathematical models is a Standard for Mathematical Practice, and specific modeling standards appear throughout the high school standards indicated by a star symbol (★). The star symbol sometimes appears on the heading for a group of standards; in that case, it should be understood to apply to all standards in that group.

BDE1FB10DFE601317A1D68A86D17958E.description: Explain why the sum or product of two rational numbers is rational; that the sum of a rational number and an irrational number is irrational; and that the product of a nonzero rational number and an irrational number is irrational.
