comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.
BC532D70DFE6013177F768A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

BC52E400DFE6013177F668A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

BC5180C0DFE6013177F268A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

BC50E0E0DFE6013177F068A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: New Jersey Common Core State Standards for English Language Arts and Literacy

C254C330DFE6013182E768A86D17958E.description: Acquire and use accurately general academic and domain-specific words and phrases, sufficient for reading, writing, speaking, and listening at the college and career readiness level; demonstrate independence in gathering vocabulary knowledge when considering a word or phrase important to comprehension or expression.

C25468E0DFE6013182E668A86D17958E.description: Analyze nuances in the meaning of words with similar denotations.

C2540D30DFE6013182E568A86D17958E.description: Interpret figures of speech (e.g., hyperbole, paradox) in context and analyze their role in the text.

C253A7A0DFE6013182E468A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.

C2533E90DFE6013182E368A86D17958E.description: Verify the preliminary determination of the meaning of a word or phrase (e.g., by checking the inferred meaning in context or in a dictionary).

C252BBB0DFE6013182E268A86D17958E.description: Consult general and specialized reference materials (e.g., dictionaries, glossaries, thesauruses), both print and digital, to find the pronunciation of a word or determine or clarify its precise meaning, its part of speech, its etymology, or its standard usage.

C2526B40DFE6013182E168A86D17958E.description: Identify and correctly use patterns of word changes that indicate different meanings or parts of speech (e.g., conceive, conception, conceivable).

C2521910DFE6013182E068A86D17958E.description: Use context (e.g., the overall meaning of a sentence, paragraph, or text; a word's position or function in a sentence) as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.

C251BC20DFE6013182DF68A86D17958E.description: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases based on grades 11—12 reading and content, choosing flexibly from a range of strategies.

C2510E80DFE6013182DD68A86D17958E.description: Vary syntax for effect, consulting references (e.g., Tufte's Artful Sentences) for guidance as needed; apply an understanding of syntax to the study of complex texts when reading.

C250BF40DFE6013182DC68A86D17958E.description: Apply knowledge of language to understand how language functions in different contexts, to make effective choices for meaning or style, and to comprehend more fully when reading or listening.

C24F64B0DFE6013182D868A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.

C24F09E0DFE6013182D768A86D17958E.description: Resolve issues of complex or contested usage, consulting references (e.g., Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage, Garner's Modern American Usage) as needed.

C24EB140DFE6013182D668A86D17958E.description: Apply the understanding that usage is a matter of convention, can change over time, and is sometimes contested.

C24E6120DFE6013182D568A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.

C24CC5B0DFE6013182D168A86D17958E.description: Acquire and use accurately a range of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases sufficient for reading, writing, speaking, and listening at the college and career readiness level; demonstrate independence in gathering vocabulary knowledge when considering a word or phrase important to comprehension or expression.

C24C7100DFE6013182D068A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.

C24C19F0DFE6013182CF68A86D17958E.description: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases by using context clues, analyzing meaningful word parts, and consulting general and specialized reference materials, as appropriate.

C24B7870DFE6013182CD68A86D17958E.description: Apply knowledge of language to understand how language functions in different contexts, to make effective choices for meaning or style, and to comprehend more fully when reading or listening.

C24ACC10DFE6013182CB68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.

C24A71C0DFE6013182CA68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.

C249BAC0DFE6013182C868A86D17958E.description: College and Career Readiness Anchor Standards for Language

C2496380DFE6013182C768A86D17958E.description: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when indicated or appropriate.

C2491060DFE6013182C668A86D17958E.description: Make strategic use of digital media (e.g., textual, graphical, audio, visual, and interactive elements) in presentations to enhance understanding of findings, reasoning, and evidence and to add interest.

C248B470DFE6013182C568A86D17958E.description: Present information, findings, and supporting evidence, conveying a clear and distinct perspective, such that listeners can follow the line of reasoning, alternative or opposing perspectives are addressed, and the organization, development, substance, and style are appropriate to purpose, audience, and a range of formal and informal tasks.

C2481680DFE6013182C368A86D17958E.description: Evaluate a speaker's point of view, reasoning, and use of evidence and rhetoric, assessing the stance, premises, links among ideas, word choice, points of emphasis, and tone used.

C247AEC0DFE6013182C268A86D17958E.description: Integrate multiple sources of information presented in diverse formats and media (e.g., visually, quantitatively, orally) in order to make informed decisions and solve problems, evaluating the credibility and accuracy of each source and noting any discrepancies among the data.

C2473E40DFE6013182C168A86D17958E.description: Respond thoughtfully to diverse perspectives; synthesize comments, claims, and evidence made on all sides of an issue; resolve contradictions when possible; and determine what additional information or research is required to deepen the investigation or complete the task.

C246F210DFE6013182C068A86D17958E.description: Propel conversations by posing and responding to questions that probe reasoning and evidence; ensure a hearing for a full range of positions on a topic or issue; clarify, verify, or challenge ideas and conclusions; and promote divergent and creative perspectives.

C246A620DFE6013182BF68A86D17958E.description: Work with peers to promote civil, democratic discussions and decision-making, set clear goals and deadlines, and establish individual roles as needed.

C2465840DFE6013182BE68A86D17958E.description: Come to discussions prepared, having read and researched material under study; explicitly draw on that preparation by referring to evidence from texts and other research on the topic or issue to stimulate a thoughtful, well-reasoned exchange of ideas.

C24608D0DFE6013182BD68A86D17958E.description: Initiate and participate effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grades 11—12 topics, texts, and issues, building on others' ideas and expressing their own clearly and persuasively.

C244FAC0DFE6013182BA68A86D17958E.description: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and communicative tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when indicated or appropriate.

C2449FA0DFE6013182B968A86D17958E.description: Make strategic use of digital media and visual displays of data to express information and enhance understanding of presentations.

C24447C0DFE6013182B868A86D17958E.description: Present information, findings, and supporting evidence such that listeners can follow the line of reasoning and the organization, development, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.

C2439B10DFE6013182B668A86D17958E.description: Evaluate a speaker's point of view, reasoning, and use of evidence and rhetoric.

C24346E0DFE6013182B568A86D17958E.description: Integrate and evaluate information presented in diverse media and formats, including visually, quantitatively, and orally.

C242F430DFE6013182B468A86D17958E.description: Prepare for and participate effectively in a range of conversations and collaborations with diverse partners, building on others' ideas and expressing their own clearly and persuasively.

C2422F90DFE6013182B268A86D17958E.description: College and Career Readiness Anchor Standards for Speaking and Listening

C241D980DFE6013182B168A86D17958E.description: Write routinely over extended time frames (time for reflection and revision) and shorter time frames (a single sitting or a day or two) for a range of discipline-specific tasks, purposes, and audiences.

C2414170DFE6013182AF68A86D17958E.description: Draw evidence from informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.

C2409AC0DFE6013182AD68A86D17958E.description: Conduct short as well as more sustained research projects to answer a question (including a self-generated question) or solve a problem; narrow or broaden the inquiry when appropriate; synthesize multiple sources on the subject, demonstrating understanding of the subject under investigation.

C2403FC0DFE6013182AC68A86D17958E.description: Research to Build and Present Knowledge

C23FEFB0DFE6013182AB68A86D17958E.description: Use technology, including the Internet, to produce, publish, and update individual or shared writing products in response to ongoing feedback, including new arguments or information.

C23F9EB0DFE6013182AA68A86D17958E.description: Develop and strengthen writing as needed by planning, revising, editing, rewriting, or trying a new approach, focusing on addressing what is most significant for a specific purpose and audience.

C23F4B60DFE6013182A968A86D17958E.description: Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.

C23E9A00DFE6013182A768A86D17958E.description: Provide a concluding statement or section that follows from and supports the information or explanation provided (e.g., articulating implications or the significance of the topic).

C23E4930DFE6013182A668A86D17958E.description: Use precise language, domain-specific vocabulary and techniques such as metaphor, simile, and analogy to manage the complexity of the topic; convey a knowledgeable stance in a style that responds to the discipline and context as well as to the expertise of likely readers.

C23DF440DFE6013182A568A86D17958E.description: Use varied transitions and sentence structures to link the major sections of the text, create cohesion, and clarify the relationships among complex ideas and concepts.

C23DA030DFE6013182A468A86D17958E.description: Develop the topic thoroughly by selecting the most significant and relevant facts, extended definitions, concrete details, quotations, or other information and examples appropriate to the audience's knowledge of the topic.

C192A990DFE60131816568A86D17958E.description: Determine a theme or central idea of a text and analyze in detail its development over the course of the text, including how it emerges and is shaped and refined by specific details; provide an objective summary of the text.

C1924D10DFE60131816468A86D17958E.description: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.

C190FF20DFE60131816168A86D17958E.description: Read and comprehend complex literary and informational texts independently and proficiently.

C190B020DFE60131816068A86D17958E.description: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity

C1905FD0DFE60131815F68A86D17958E.description: Analyze how two or more texts address similar themes or topics in order to build knowledge or to compare the approaches the authors take.

C1901090DFE60131815E68A86D17958E.description: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, including the validity of the reasoning as well as the relevance and sufficiency of the evidence.

C18FAFE0DFE60131815D68A86D17958E.description: Integrate and evaluate content presented in diverse media and formats, including visually and quantitatively, as well as in words.

C18F1970DFE60131815B68A86D17958E.description: Assess how point of view or purpose shapes the content and style of a text.

C18ECD30DFE60131815A68A86D17958E.description: Analyze the structure of texts, including how specific sentences, paragraphs, and larger portions of the text (e.g., a section, chapter, scene, or stanza) relate to each other and the whole.

C18E80F0DFE60131815968A86D17958E.description: Interpret words and phrases as they are used in a text, including determining technical, connotative, and figurative meanings, and analyze how specific word choices shape meaning or tone.

C18DD770DFE60131815768A86D17958E.description: Analyze how and why individuals, events, and ideas develop and interact over the course of a text.

C18D8590DFE60131815668A86D17958E.description: Determine central ideas or themes of a text and analyze their development; summarize the key supporting details and ideas.

C18D3390DFE60131815568A86D17958E.description: Read closely to determine what the text says explicitly and to make logical inferences from it; cite specific textual evidence when writing or speaking to support conclusions drawn from the text.

FC8FA0496C25486F8982DA714CF43241.description: Respect and acceptance for individuals regardless of gender, sexual orientation, disability, ethnicity, socioeconomic background, religion, and/or culture provide a foundation for the prevention and resolution of conflict.

A679917239234F52B0FF1242241B3A3D.description: Social and emotional development impacts all components of wellness.

BEC823FE67D3464AAA183985EE5215D7.description: Compare and contrast common mental illnesses (such as depression, anxiety and panic disorders, and phobias) and ways to detect and treat them.

document.title: New Jersey Common Core State Standards for English Language Arts and Literacy

C07D5770DFE601317FB568A86D17958E.description: Acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases; gather vocabulary knowledge when considering a word or phrase important to comprehension or expression.

C07CDE00DFE601317FB468A86D17958E.description: Distinguish among the connotations (associations) of words with similar denotations (definitions) (e.g., stingy, scrimping, economical, unwasteful, thrifty).

C07C90F0DFE601317FB368A86D17958E.description: Use the relationship between particular words (e.g., cause/effect, part/whole, item/category) to better understand each of the words.

C07C4120DFE601317FB268A86D17958E.description: Interpret figures of speech (e.g., personification) in context.

C07BF080DFE601317FB168A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.

C07BA2C0DFE601317FB068A86D17958E.description: Verify the preliminary determination of the meaning of a word or phrase (e.g., by checking the inferred meaning in context or in a dictionary).

C07B5030DFE601317FAF68A86D17958E.description: Consult reference materials (e.g., dictionaries, glossaries, thesauruses), both print and digital, to find the pronunciation of a word or determine or clarify its precise meaning or its part of speech.

C07AFF80DFE601317FAE68A86D17958E.description: Use common, grade-appropriate Greek or Latin affixes and roots as clues to the meaning of a word (e.g., audience, auditory, audible).

C07AAE00DFE601317FAD68A86D17958E.description: Use context (e.g., the overall meaning of a sentence or paragraph; a word's position or function in a sentence) as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.

C07A5AB0DFE601317FAC68A86D17958E.description: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases based on grade 6 reading and content, choosing flexibly from a range of strategies.

C079A270DFE601317FAA68A86D17958E.description: Maintain consistency in style and tone.

C07936B0DFE601317FA968A86D17958E.description: Vary sentence patterns for meaning, reader/listener interest, and style.

C078DEA0DFE601317FA868A86D17958E.description: Use knowledge of language and its conventions when writing, speaking, reading, or listening.

C077F1F0DFE601317FA568A86D17958E.description: Use punctuation (commas, parentheses, dashes) to set off nonrestrictive/parenthetical elements.

C07793B0DFE601317FA468A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.

C0774420DFE601317FA368A86D17958E.description: Recognize variations from standard English in their own and others' writing and speaking, and identify and use strategies to improve expression in conventional language.

C076F760DFE601317FA268A86D17958E.description: Recognize and correct vague pronouns (i.e., ones with unclear or ambiguous antecedents).

C076A320DFE601317FA168A86D17958E.description: Recognize and correct inappropriate shifts in pronoun number and person.

C075F290DFE601317F9F68A86D17958E.description: Ensure that pronouns are in the proper case (subjective, objective, possessive).

C075A340DFE601317F9E68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.

C07428D0DFE601317F9A68A86D17958E.description: Acquire and use accurately a range of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases sufficient for reading, writing, speaking, and listening at the college and career readiness level; demonstrate independence in gathering vocabulary knowledge when considering a word or phrase important to comprehension or expression.

C073C900DFE601317F9968A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.

C07379E0DFE601317F9868A86D17958E.description: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases by using context clues, analyzing meaningful word parts, and consulting general and specialized reference materials, as appropriate.

C072D7C0DFE601317F9668A86D17958E.description: Apply knowledge of language to understand how language functions in different contexts, to make effective choices for meaning or style, and to comprehend more fully when reading or listening.

C07214D0DFE601317F9468A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.

C07195F0DFE601317F9368A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.

C070F3C0DFE601317F9168A86D17958E.description: College and Career Readiness Anchor Standards for Language

C07096C0DFE601317F9068A86D17958E.description: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when indicated or appropriate.

C0704A40DFE601317F8F68A86D17958E.description: Include multimedia components (e.g., graphics, images, music, sound) and visual displays in presentations to clarify information.

C06FFCC0DFE601317F8E68A86D17958E.description: Present claims and findings, sequencing ideas logically and using pertinent descriptions, facts, and details to accentuate main ideas or themes; use appropriate eye contact, adequate volume, and clear pronunciation.

C06F5350DFE601317F8C68A86D17958E.description: Delineate a speaker's argument and specific claims, distinguishing claims that are supported by reasons and evidence from claims that are not.

C06EFB30DFE601317F8B68A86D17958E.description: Interpret information presented in diverse media and formats (e.g., visually, quantitatively, orally) and explain how it contributes to a topic, text, or issue under study.

C06E8E80DFE601317F8A68A86D17958E.description: Review the key ideas expressed and demonstrate understanding of multiple perspectives through reflection and paraphrasing.

C06E43E0DFE601317F8968A86D17958E.description: Pose and respond to specific questions with elaboration and detail by making comments that contribute to the topic, text, or issue under discussion.

C06DF870DFE601317F8868A86D17958E.description: Follow rules for collegial discussions, set specific goals and deadlines, and define individual roles as needed.

C06DAAE0DFE601317F8768A86D17958E.description: Come to discussions prepared, having read or studied required material; explicitly draw on that preparation by referring to evidence on the topic, text, or issue to probe and reflect on ideas under discussion.

C06D5DA0DFE601317F8668A86D17958E.description: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grade 6 topics, texts, and issues, building on others' ideas and expressing their own clearly.

C06C4380DFE601317F8368A86D17958E.description: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and communicative tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when indicated or appropriate.

C06BCC70DFE601317F8268A86D17958E.description: Make strategic use of digital media and visual displays of data to express information and enhance understanding of presentations.

C06B7C80DFE601317F8168A86D17958E.description: Present information, findings, and supporting evidence such that listeners can follow the line of reasoning and the organization, development, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.

C06ACB00DFE601317F7F68A86D17958E.description: Evaluate a speaker's point of view, reasoning, and use of evidence and rhetoric.

C06A7120DFE601317F7E68A86D17958E.description: Integrate and evaluate information presented in diverse media and formats, including visually, quantitatively, and orally.

C06A19B0DFE601317F7D68A86D17958E.description: Prepare for and participate effectively in a range of conversations and collaborations with diverse partners, building on others' ideas and expressing their own clearly and persuasively.

C0697270DFE601317F7B68A86D17958E.description: College and Career Readiness Anchor Standards for Speaking and Listening

C068FD00DFE601317F7A68A86D17958E.description: Write routinely over extended time frames (time for reflection and revision) and shorter time frames (a single sitting or a day or two) for a range of discipline-specific tasks, purposes, and audiences.

C06862E0DFE601317F7868A86D17958E.description: Draw evidence from informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.

C0680EB0DFE601317F7768A86D17958E.description: Gather relevant information from multiple print and digital sources, using search terms effectively; assess the credibility and accuracy of each source; and quote or paraphrase the data and conclusions of others while avoiding plagiarism and following a standard format for citation.

B05ED67B50A848A0A4B1A6E9F5DED55F.description: Effective communication may be a determining factor in the outcome of health- and safety-related situations.

AC643CDA73C342409569ABF8D38ED61A.description: Integrated Skills: All students will develop and use personal and interpersonal skills to support a healthy, active lifestyle.

CB2EE66C82C640A5B1A9461BAC26D12C.description: Identify basic social and emotional needs of all people.

document.title: New Jersey Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

BCCF8450DFE6013178C268A86D17958E.description: Compare two fractions with the same numerator or the same denominator by reasoning about their size. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two fractions refer to the same whole. Record the results of comparisons with the symbols >, =, or <, and justify the conclusions, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.

comments: Example: express 3 in the form 3 = 3/1; recognize that 6/1 = 6.
Example: locate 4/4 and 1 at the same point of a number line diagram.
BCCF3530DFE6013178C168A86D17958E.description: Express whole numbers as fractions, and recognize fractions that are equivalent to whole numbers.

BCCEE7E0DFE6013178C068A86D17958E.description: Recognize and generate simple equivalent fractions, e.g., 1/2 = 2/4, 4/6 = 2/3). Explain why the fractions are equivalent, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.

BCCEA6B0DFE6013178BF68A86D17958E.description: Understand two fractions as equivalent (equal) if they are the same size, or the same point on a number line.

BCCE6500DFE6013178BE68A86D17958E.description: Explain equivalence of fractions in special cases, and compare fractions by reasoning about their size.

BCCE24E0DFE6013178BD68A86D17958E.description: Represent a fraction a/b on a number line diagram by marking off a lengths 1/b from 0. Recognize that the resulting interval has size a/b and that its endpoint locates the number a/b on the number line.

BCCDE180DFE6013178BC68A86D17958E.description: Represent a fraction 1/b on a number line diagram by defining the interval from 0 to 1 as the whole and partitioning it into b equal parts. Recognize that each part has size 1/b and that the endpoint of the part based at 0 locates the number 1/b on the number line.

BCCD99A0DFE6013178BB68A86D17958E.description: Understand a fraction as a number on the number line; represent fractions on a number line diagram.

BCCD49D0DFE6013178BA68A86D17958E.description: Understand a fraction 1/b as the quantity formed by 1 part when a whole is partitioned into b equal parts; understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b.

BCCD0620DFE6013178B968A86D17958E.description: Develop understanding of fractions as numbers.

comments: Grade 3 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 6, and 8.
Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 100

BCCC6BC0DFE6013178B768A86D17958E.description: Partition shapes into parts with equal areas. Express the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole.
comments: For example, partition a shape into 4 parts with equal area, and describe the area of each part as 1/4 of the area of the shape.

BCCC1B50DFE6013178B668A86D17958E.description: Understand that shapes in different categories (e.g., rhombuses, rectangles, and others) may share attributes (e.g., having four sides), and that the shared attributes can define a larger category (e.g., quadrilaterals). Recognize rhombuses, rectangles, and squares as examples of quadrilaterals, and draw examples of quadrilaterals that do not belong to any of these subcategories.

BCCBCA80DFE6013178B568A86D17958E.description: Reason with shapes and their attributes.

BCCB3F00DFE6013178B368A86D17958E.description: Solve real world and mathematical problems involving perimeters of polygons, including finding the perimeter given the side lengths, finding an unknown side length, and exhibiting rectangles with the same perimeter and different areas or with the same area and different perimeters.

BCCAF9D0DFE6013178B268A86D17958E.description: Geometric measurement: recognize perimeter as an attribute of plane figures and distinguish between linear and area measures.

BCCAAD90DFE6013178B168A86D17958E.description: Recognize area as additive. Find areas of rectilinear figures by decomposing them into non-overlapping rectangles and adding the areas of the non-overlapping parts, applying this technique to solve real world problems.

BCCA57A0DFE6013178B068A86D17958E.description: Use tiling to show in a concrete case that the area of a rectangle with whole-number side lengths a and b + c is the sum of a × b and a × c. Use area models to represent the distributive property in mathematical reasoning.

BCC9F7C0DFE6013178AF68A86D17958E.description: Multiply side lengths to find areas of rectangles with whole-number side lengths in the context of solving real world and mathematical problems, and represent whole-number products as rectangular areas in mathematical reasoning.

BCC9A6C0DFE6013178AE68A86D17958E.description: Find the area of a rectangle with whole-number side lengths by tiling it, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths.

BCC96250DFE6013178AD68A86D17958E.description: Relate area to the operations of multiplication and addition.

BCC91DD0DFE6013178AC68A86D17958E.description: Measure areas by counting unit squares (square cm, square m, square in, square ft, and improvised units).

BCC8D940DFE6013178AB68A86D17958E.description: A plane figure which can be covered without gaps or overlaps by n unit squares is said to have an area of n square units.

BCC893B0DFE6013178AA68A86D17958E.description: A square with side length 1 unit, called "a unit square," is said to have "one square unit" of area, and can be used to measure area.

BCC84CA0DFE6013178A968A86D17958E.description: Recognize area as an attribute of plane figures and understand concepts of area measurement.

BCC7FA20DFE6013178A868A86D17958E.description: Geometric measurement: understand concepts of area and relate area to multiplication and to addition.

BCC6B650DFE6013178A468A86D17958E.description: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths using rulers marked with halves and fourths of an inch. Show the data by making a line plot, where the horizontal scale is marked off in appropriate units— whole numbers, halves, or quarters.

comments: For example, draw a bar graph in which each square in the bar graph might represent 5 pets.
BCC67240DFE6013178A368A86D17958E.description: Draw a scaled picture graph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set with several categories. Solve one- and two-step "how many more" and "how many less" problems using information presented in scaled bar graphs.

BCC7A520DFE6013178A768A86D17958E.description: Measure and estimate liquid volumes and masses of objects using standard units of grams (g), kilograms (kg), and liters (l). Add, subtract, multiply, or divide to solve one-step word problems involving masses or volumes that are given in the same units, e.g., by using drawings (such as a beaker with a measurement scale) to represent the problem.
comments: Excludes multiplicative comparison problems (problems involving notions of "times as much";
Excludes compound units such as cm³ and finding the geometric volume of a container.

BCC75170DFE6013178A668A86D17958E.description: Tell and write time to the nearest minute and measure time intervals in minutes. Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of time intervals in minutes, e.g., by representing the problem on a number line diagram.

BCC702D0DFE6013178A568A86D17958E.description: Solve problems involving measurement and estimation of intervals of time, liquid volumes, and masses of objects.

BCC5A480DFE6013178A068A86D17958E.description: Multiply one-digit whole numbers by multiples of 10 in the range 10—90 (e.g., 9 × 80, 5 × 60) using strategies based on place value and properties of operations.

BCC56300DFE60131789F68A86D17958E.description: Fluently add and subtract within 1000 using strategies and algorithms based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction.

BCC52160DFE60131789E68A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding to round whole numbers to the nearest 10 or 100.

BCC4D9F0DFE60131789D68A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to perform multi-digit arithmetic.
comments: A range of algorithms may be used.

BCC48180DFE60131789C68A86D17958E.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten
comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.

BCC43070DFE60131789B68A86D17958E.description: Identify arithmetic patterns (including patterns in the addition table or multiplication table), and explain them using properties of operations.
comments: For example, observe that 4 times a number is always even, and explain why 4 times a number can be decomposed into two equal addends.

BCC3EF60DFE60131789A68A86D17958E.description: Solve two-step word problems using the four operations. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.
comments: This standard is limited to problems posed with whole numbers and having whole-number answers; students should know how to perform operations in the conventional order when there are no parentheses to specify a particular order (Order of Operations).

BCC3AEF0DFE60131789968A86D17958E.description: Solve problems involving the four operations, and identify and explain patterns in arithmetic.

BCC36980DFE60131789868A86D17958E.description: Fluently multiply and divide within 100, using strategies such as the relationship between multiplication and division (e.g., knowing that 8 × 5 = 40, one knows 40 ÷ 5 = 8) or properties of operations. By the end of Grade 3, know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers.

comments: For example, find 32 ÷ 8 by finding the number that makes 32 when multiplied by 8.
BCC2DBF0DFE60131789668A86D17958E.description: Understand division as an unknown-factor problem.

comments: Students need not use formal terms for these properties.
Example: Knowing that 8 × 5 = 40 and 8 × 2 = 16, one can find 8 × 7 as 8 × (5 + 2) = (8 × 5) + (8 × 2) = 40 + 16 = 56. (Distributive property.)

Example: If 6 × 4 = 24 is known, then 4 × 6 = 24 is also known (Commutative property of multiplication.) 3 × 5 × 2 can be found by 3 × 5 = 15, then 15 × 2 = 30, or by 5 × 2 = 10, then 3 × 10 = 30. (Associative property of multiplication.)
BCC285E0DFE60131789568A86D17958E.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide.

BCC244A0DFE60131789468A86D17958E.description: Understand properties of multiplication and the relationship between multiplication and division.

BCC1FEF0DFE60131789368A86D17958E.description: Determine the unknown whole number in a multiplication or division equation relating three whole numbers.
comments: For example, determine the unknown number that makes the equation true in each of the equations 8 × ? = 48, 5 = ÷ 3, 6 × 6 = ?.

BCC1BDE0DFE60131789268A86D17958E.description: Use multiplication and division within 100 to solve word problems in situations involving equal groups, arrays, and measurement quantities, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

comments: For example, describe a context in which a number of shares or a number of groups can be expressed as 56 ÷ 8.
BCC17BC0DFE60131789168A86D17958E.description: Interpret whole-number quotients of whole numbers, e.g., interpret 56 ÷ 8 as the number of objects in each share when 56 objects are partitioned equally into 8 shares, or as a number of shares when 56 objects are partitioned into equal shares of 8 objects each.

comments: For example, describe a context in which a total number of objects can be expressed as 5 × 7.
BCC137C0DFE60131789068A86D17958E.description: Interpret products of whole numbers, e.g., interpret 5 × 7 as the total number of objects in 5 groups of 7 objects each.

BCC0EA20DFE60131788F68A86D17958E.description: Represent and solve problems involving multiplication and division.

comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.
BCC05420DFE60131788D68A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

BCBFFB40DFE60131788C68A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

BCBE6780DFE60131788868A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.
BCBDC2C0DFE60131788668A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.

document.title: New Jersey Core Curriculum Content Standards for Science (NGSS)

3CA4D2B112EE4AA5A450A00A00496994.description: Plan and carry out fair tests in which variables are controlled and failure points are considered to identify aspects of a model or prototype that can be improved.

17BF366FE0694B5CA6FB223B970CB155.description: Generate and compare multiple possible solutions to a problem based on how well each is likely to meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.

A6B2C6C9384D49A384E4D390885E6934.description: Define a simple design problem reflecting a need or a want that includes specified criteria for success and constraints on materials, time, or cost.

20A04D5F629D457C818234D7BFF66415.description: Make a claim about the merit of a design solution that reduces the impacts of a weather-related hazard.
comments: Clarification Statement: Examples of design solutions to weather-related hazards could include barriers to prevent flooding, wind resistant roofs, and lighting rods.

38964CCBC1A04E318A68FAF5DAA61DEB.description: Obtain and combine information to describe climates in different regions of the world.

comments: Clarification Statement: Examples of data could include average temperature, precipitation, and wind direction.
Assessment Boundary: Assessment of graphical displays is limited to pictographs and bar graphs. Assessment does not include climate change.
B0D92033660E4202B5B945171224660D.description: Represent data in tables and graphical displays to describe typical weather conditions expected during a particular season.

FB8C4299A1454577985A144FEFA53E11.description: Make a claim about the merit of a solution to a problem caused when the environment changes and the types of plants and animals that live there may change.
comments: Clarification Statement: Examples of environmental changes could include changes in land characteristics, water distribution, temperature, food, and other organisms.
Assessment Boundary: Assessment is limited to a single environmental change. Assessment does not include the greenhouse effect or climate change.

Clarification Statement: Examples of evidence could include needs and characteristics of the organisms and habitats involved. The organisms and their habitat make up a system in which the parts depend on each other.
A039E0F097D845328CC084FC1C96AB56.description: Construct an argument with evidence that in a particular habitat some organisms can survive well, some survive less well, and some cannot survive at all.

comments: Clarification Statement: Examples of cause and effect relationships could be plants that have larger thorns than other plants may be less likely to be eaten by predators; and, animals that have better camouflage coloration than other animals may be more likely to survive and therefore more likely to leave offspring.
1F33F9427C8D4F27BB5D01BBB8E88CDB.description: Use evidence to construct an explanation for how the variations in characteristics among individuals of the same species may provide advantages in surviving, finding mates, and reproducing.

DA1203E6403A4F01BD963ACF6509C663.description: Analyze and interpret data from fossils to provide evidence of the organisms and the environments in which they lived long ago.
comments: Clarification Statement: Examples of data could include type, size, and distributions of fossil organisms. Examples of fossils and environments could include marine fossils found on dry land, tropical plant fossils found in Arctic areas, and fossils of extinct organisms.
Assessment Boundary: Assessment does not include identification of specific fossils or present plants and animals. Assessment is limited to major fossil types and relative ages.

5C3D59E34DE7463CBFE7E8FBD9C58E00.description: Use evidence to support the explanation that traits can be influenced by the environment.
comments: Clarification Statement: Examples of the environment affecting a trait could include normally tall plants grown with insufficient water are stunted; and, a pet dog that is given too much food and little exercise may become overweight.

315ED88CDEA24BBEA8C2B11E7ACEE6F0.description: Analyze and interpret data to provide evidence that plants and animals have traits inherited from parents and that variation of these traits exists in a group of similar organisms.
comments: Clarification Statement: Patterns are the similarities and differences in traits shared between offspring and their parents, or among siblings. Emphasis is on organisms other than humans.
Assessment Boundary: Assessment does not include genetic mechanisms of inheritance and prediction of traits. Assessment is limited to non-human examples.

DDEA740EE6044749A96ADE3D5536E9A2.description: Heredity: Inheritance and Variation of Traits

9F68C5582D7E435593A2F72C1E35B7A3.description: Construct an argument that some animals form groups that help members survive.

3AF5AD44BE2F44E1A5ACBA7C3F947BC8.description: Develop models to describe that organisms have unique and diverse life cycles but all have in common birth, growth, reproduction, and death.
comments: Clarification Statement: Changes organisms go through during their life form a pattern.
Assessment Boundary: Assessment of plant life cycles is limited to those of flowering plants. Assessment does not include details of human reproduction.

EAF6EDE6437F444BA5A89038A81D44B3.description: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes

744AAF448F944F71A93631CD798C1811.description: Define a simple design problem that can be solved by applying scientific ideas about magnets.
comments: Clarification Statement: Examples of problems could include constructing a latch to keep a door shut and creating a device to keep two moving objects from touching each other.

E067EC96BED74BBA983D23438220F9B4.description: Ask questions to determine cause and effect relationships of electric or magnetic interactions between two objects not in contact with each other.
comments: Clarification Statement: Examples of an electric force could include the force on hair from an electrically charged balloon and the electrical forces between a charged rod and pieces of paper; examples of a magnetic force could include the force between two permanent magnets, the force between an electromagnet and steel paperclips, and the force exerted by one magnet versus the force exerted by two magnets. Examples of cause and effect relationships could include how the distance between objects affects strength of the force and how the orientation of magnets affects the direction of the magnetic force.
Assessment Boundary: Assessment is limited to forces produced by objects that can be manipulated by students, and electrical interactions are limited to static electricity.

F7FD863F9F074BA2B90EFFF7D40808FF.description: Make observations and/or measurements of an object's motion to provide evidence that a pattern can be used to predict future motion.
comments: Clarification Statement: Examples of motion with a predictable pattern could include a child swinging in a swing, a ball rolling back and forth in a bowl, and two children on a see-saw.
Assessment Boundary: Assessment does not include technical terms such as period and frequency.

B954E4321C4E44E1B9BD7B80A14B5DBF.description: Plan and conduct an investigation to provide evidence of the effects of balanced and unbalanced forces on the motion of an object.
comments: Clarification Statement: Examples could include an unbalanced force on one side of a ball can make it start moving; and, balanced forces pushing on a box from both sides will not produce any motion at all.

Assessment Boundary: Assessment is limited to one variable at a time: number, size, or direction of forces. Assessment does not include quantitative force size, only qualitative and relative. Assessment is limited to gravity being addressed as a force that pulls objects down.

4AAB1A75D17346D69522BE6EB07AF425.description: Motion and Stability: Forces and Interactions

document.title: New Jersey Core Curriculum Content Standards for Visual and Performing Arts

83F2EF4E41074DFD9B5DD0365805B64D.description: Distinguish ways in which individuals may disagree about the relative merits and effectiveness of artistic choices in the creation and performance of works of dance, music, theatre, and visual art.

75A0500C050E41088DFD5E3E92A03175.description: Artists and audiences can and do disagree about the relative merits of artwork. When assessing works of dance, music, theatre and visual art, it is important to consider the context for the creation and performance of the work (e.g., Who was the creator? What purpose does the artwork serve? Who is the intended audience?).

2C3EA49335614F1BA6E1A0838CCA6B5E.description: Define technical proficiency, using the elements of the arts and principles of design.

7221E0AAE7E44994A4369BD187EA639F.description: Levels of proficiency can be assessed through analyses of how artists apply the elements of art and principles of design.

9C35BE125DF440DAB0E7BAC1AD627D63.description: Use discipline-specific arts terminology to evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of works of dance, music, theatre, and visual art.

1448A0A1CC884178A52B3080F32DCFFE.description: While there is shared vocabulary among the four arts disciplines of dance, music, theatre, and visual art, each also has its own discipline-specific arts terminology.

F36269A1C16B4776A6FD6CD857BDBF19.description: Use evaluative tools, such as rubrics, for self-assessment and to appraise the objectivity of critiques by peers.

107FAB58D16240479C88C0E2F96CB542.description: Decoding simple contextual clues requires evaluation mechanisms, such as rubrics, to sort fact from opinion.

7AA7F5E013714D16B9FB5ABBFCE490D5.description: Assess the application of the elements of art and principles of design in dance, music, theatre, and visual artworks using observable, objective criteria.

7F960177A1C647B8849F6429E957D71D.description: Identifying criteria for evaluating performances results in deeper understanding of art and art-making.

B79811F4DAF64C5F9D59943C355D0D2A.description: Demonstrate how art communicates ideas about personal and social values and is inspired by an individual's imagination and frame of reference (e.g., personal, social, political, historical context).

F38D59EA40284A44B10DDFFFC0405287.description: Criteria for determining the aesthetic merits of artwork vary according to context. Understanding the relationship between compositional design and genre provides the foundation for making value judgments about the arts.

AB0DB22D970F4BF98099A6DA7C3F487A.description: Make informed aesthetic responses to artworks based on structural arrangement and personal, cultural, and historical points of view.

2D06D5E4872842FCAEFDE9E34F8D9510.description: Formalism in dance, music, theatre, and visual art varies according to personal, cultural, and historical contexts.

EB3DF98AF6844079AE11B54A7B55058D.description: Employ basic, discipline-specific arts terminology to categorize works of dance, music, theatre, and visual art according to established classifications.

4C05D04FDD1A4C56903FAC200E3F677F.description: Works of art may be organized according to their functions and artistic purposes (e.g., genres, mediums, messages, themes).

30B76765981547A0A17C0D63E2E7F579.description: Aesthetic Responses & Critique Methodologies: All students will demonstrate and apply an understanding of arts philosophies, judgment, and analysis to works of art in dance, music, theatre, and visual art.

6F92B2891BD24DB78DCCC668D06B4451.description: Collaborate in the creation of works of art using multiple art media and art mediums, and present the completed works in exhibition areas inside and outside the classroom.

DEEF972EDFF14EFBA0F94E33E4FF2C6F.description: There are many types of aesthetic arrangements for the exhibition of art. Creating or assembling gallery exhibitions requires effective time management and creative problem-solving skills.

CD83439FFB084638B0757DF1DAF26960.description: Differentiate drawing, painting, ceramics, sculpture, printmaking, textiles, and computer imaging by the physical properties of the resulting artworks, and experiment with various art media and art mediums to create original works of art.

5A4A3B2A7CBF4062AAA86F5385C49B96.description: The characteristics and physical properties of the various materials available for use in art-making present infinite possibilities for potential application.

A2EFC32ECA4E4FF8BE8424CC179190AC.description: Identify common and distinctive characteristics of genres of visual artworks (e.g., realism, surrealism, abstract/nonobjective art, conceptual art, and others) using age-appropriate terminology, and experiment with various compositional approaches influenced by these genres.

4DEE08C5D98647A18C3151F1392300D7.description: Each of the genres of visual art (e.g., realism, surrealism, abstract/nonobjective art, conceptual art, and others) is associated with appropriate vocabulary and a stylistic approach to art-making.

B63124A3625041C5AED440380EB07118.description: Identify common and distinctive characteristics of artworks from diverse cultural and historical eras of visual art using age-appropriate stylistic terminology (e.g., cubist, surreal, optic, impressionistic), and experiment with various compositional approaches influenced by these styles.

AC276BDCE679403D9A37F9F7A8347C77.description: Contextual clues to culturally specific thematic content, symbolism, compositional approach, and stylistic nuance are prevalent in works of art throughout the ages.

8A43CD4BA7994C3B82C06ACC8A50C234.description: Work individually and collaboratively to create two- and three-dimensional works of art that make cohesive visual statements and that employ the elements of art and principles of design.

AEBE29483B7F4F50AFCB2929E7EA4339.description: The elements of art and principles of design can be applied in an infinite number of ways to express personal responses to creative problems.

30D2703007DD4A0A8035E419B71F7961.description: Demonstrate how active listening skills, vocal variety, physical expression, stage business, sensory recall, concentration, and focus affect meaning in scripted and improvised performances.

386C9B35E96D4BE7B0D9722BE8259ED8.description: Performers use active listening skills in scripted and improvised performances to create believable, multidimensional characters. Actors create a sense of truth and believability by applying performance techniques that are appropriate to the circumstances of a scripted or improvised performance.

EE6B0735E7A34BAEA22B60442A7D14C1.description: Create original plays using script-writing formats that include stage directions and technical theatrical elements, demonstrating comprehension of the elements of theatre and story construction.

3B12C725C00748DDB18EBFADB477AA2F.description: A play's effectiveness is enhanced by the theatre artists' knowledge of technical theatrical elements and understanding of the elements of theatre.

7A8B8BABE9104FEAAED41384F4B69C31.description: Decode how the elements of music are used to achieve unity and variety, tension and release, and balance in musical compositions.

E50B482D8F4A424387580CF2F5D7A29D.description: Decoding musical scores requires understanding of notation systems, the elements of music, and basic compositional concepts.

D069F3CD37EF45D99C4C986D14042C21.description: Improvise and score simple melodies over given harmonic structures using traditional instruments and/or computer programs.

39AAAD76BCA94938A1E32F6905223B53.description: Music composition is governed by prescribed rules and forms that apply to both improvised and scored music.

9889FBE3F96242598B5DA0904AFDB2F5.description: Sing melodic and harmonizing parts, independently and in groups, adjusting to the range and timbre of the developing voice.

9EEB5BBD2DCB4AE7A67E592FE937E403.description: Proper vocal production and vocal placement improve vocal quality. Harmonizing requires singing ability and active listening skills. Individual voice ranges change with time.

5C4DDECB914F40D087F901A39F14B494.description: Sing or play music from complex notation, using notation systems in treble and bass clef, mixed meter, and compound meter.

E49D699196A948829CCDBE9B879D3A64.description: Complex scores may include compound meters and the grand staff.

EE194EA2C24D4C7B9424AE7FA03773F2.description: Perform basic sequences of movement from different styles or traditions accurately, demonstrating proper alignment, balance, initiation of movement, and direction of focus.

061A23435F0C4BFD95DA7187FBB4DBF5.description: Various dance styles, traditions, and techniques adhere to basic principles of alignment, balance, focus, and initiation of movement.

E770ACB45F9E432D949C1E26D56C6F44.description: Demonstrate developmentally appropriate kinesthetic awareness of basic anatomical principles, using flexibility, balance, strength, focus, concentration, and coordination.

4A869838AFC645099CB6285AF5261B6D.description: Dance requires a fundamental understanding of body alignment and applied kinesthetic principles. Age-appropriate conditioning of the body enhances flexibility, balance, strength, focus, concentration, and performance technique.

ED8CC35D04574171A6DB2176C62DA2E0.description: Create and perform dances alone and in small groups that communicate meaning on a variety of themes, using props or artwork as creative stimuli.

5BF10A2F6B6441EBA260AABFD5722675.description: Works of art, props, and other creative stimuli can be used to inform the thematic content of dances.

CA75D81A6E6E42AABCFD97FD432AE141.description: Use improvisation as a tool to create and perform movement sequences incorporating various spatial levels (i.e., low, middle, and high), tempos, and spatial pathways.

88666E5F93F84064AB45AE111A8A39E9.description: The creation of an original dance composition is often reliant on improvisation as a choreographic tool. The essence/character of a movement sequence is also transformed when performed at varying spatial levels (i.e., low, middle, and high), at different tempos, along different spatial pathways, or with different movement qualities.

19E3208B5F654566AAC5E7129D5D9DA6.description: Perform planned and improvised sequences with a distinct beginning, middle, and end that manipulate time, space, and energy, and accurately transfer rhythmic patterns from the auditory to the kinesthetic.

FB21845E9E1C4E2E8C310F342B8684D6.description: Fundamental movement structures include a defined beginning, middle, and ending. Planned choreographic and improvised movement sequences manipulate time, space, and energy. Kinesthetic transference of rhythm comes from auditory and visual stimuli.

183C7E0B4CC34883B6969F02B9F1AB65.description: Performance: All students will synthesize those skills, media, methods, and technologies appropriate to creating, performing, and/or presenting works of art in dance, music, theatre, and visual art.

498CFF2EDFFF48D9BFCF645FFD7A7078.description: Determine the impact of significant contributions of individual artists in dance, music, theatre, and visual art from diverse cultures throughout history.

5DD04BCE9217490DA41A18C72460652A.description: Sometimes the contributions of an individual artist can influence a generation of artists and signal the beginning of a new art genre.

966424B9534040E4BAD63922224CCAD3.description: Relate common artistic elements that define distinctive art genres in dance, music, theatre, and visual art.

AE2228D7BAEB4E19A95E8CDE94AA2B4C.description: Characteristic approaches to content, form, style, and design define art genres.

54FD0061483D479FA11BC2A73ED489E3.description: Recognize works of dance, music, theatre, and visual art as a reflection of societal values and beliefs.

F5A0747C081B4DD8B2813E8791F38C65.description: Art and culture reflect and affect each other.

16E973AF8EB1453BB6B27290A276A94B.description: History of the Arts and Culture

D8A9D9A1E97441998F493891299697CE.description: History of the Arts and Culture: All students will understand the role, development, and influence of the arts throughout history and across cultures.

85A56BBD1EDE419D868A8A65DEC36858.description: Compare and contrast works of art in various mediums that use the same art elements and principles of design.

E29C5DFD4E7B4C20B98F8158B3C1235E.description: The elements of art and principles of design are universal.

03995237F2D245039852CA4A82D2E757.description: Identify elements of art and principles of design that are evident in everyday life.

59DD1725C5484C72BEBB912AFB36895A.description: Understanding the function and purpose of the elements of art and principles of design assists with forming an appreciation of how art and design enhance functionality and improve quality of living.

2CCCEE91F9FF48E9AB6857C07BBB8886.description: Explain the function of sensory recall and apply it to character development.

80617FDD451647098E9977183BEE4EC3.description: Sensory recall is a technique actors commonly employ to heighten the believability of a character.

4D2A3E0EB59049CF84E67A4BCC740551.description: Analyze the use of technical theatrical elements to identify how time, place, mood, and theme are created.

1B3E0D0746E14E41A020CE1624546D98.description: Time, place, mood, and theme are enhanced through use of the technical theatrical elements.

4595CB9F3FB848A3A73C7432157468E7.description: Interpret the relationship between the actor's physical and vocal choices and an audience's perception of character development by identifying examples of vocal variety, stage business, concentration, and focus.

05FF153406954C8C8397E348EE6CC322.description: The actor's physicality and vocal techniques have a direct relationship to character development.

83C529301988455288E2F142A4091BA9.description: Evaluate the characteristics of a well-made play in a variety of scripts and performances.

E8C3143B8AA24E0688A47BC8227B6FE5.description: The well-made play uses a specific, identifiable narrative structure (e.g., inciting incident, climax, dénouement, etc.).

669493777C8A497EA3617CD4E4C04EE2.description: Demonstrate the basic concepts of meter, rhythm, tonality, intervals, chords, and melodic and harmonic progressions, and differentiate basic structures.

800BA8AD3FC44060BE04722029575229.description: Reading basic music notation contributes to musical fluency and literacy. Musical intelligence is related to ear training and listening skill, and temporal spatial reasoning ability is connected to listening skill.

676E690887664BCE8085FC93A235C238.description: Differentiate contrasting and complimentary shapes, shared weight centers, body parts, body patterning, balance, and range of motion in compositions and performances.

07FCCD560A2F4ACD8E2BD8EB01B3A900.description: Determine how accompaniment (such as sound, spoken text, or silence) can affect choreography and improvisation.

F4BC077A3CAB4387930E82EC7EF646AC.description: Musical and non-musical forms of sound can affect meaning in choreography and improvisation.

15CB04D8E1214896BD260AB343E7D0D6.description: Movement is developed and generated through improvisation. Form and structure are important when interpreting original choreography.

891645601B0A49EF89F8D89866965E34.description: Basic choreographed structures employ the elements of dance.
