document.title: New Jersey Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

BC878310DFE60131784F68A86D17958E.description: Partition circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares, describe the shares using the words halves, fourths, and quarters, and use the phrases half of, fourth of, and quarter of. Describe the whole as two of, or four of the shares. Understand for these examples that decomposing into more equal shares creates smaller shares.

comments: Students do not need to learn formal names such as "right rectangular prism."
BC8732A0DFE60131784E68A86D17958E.description: Compose two-dimensional shapes (rectangles, squares, trapezoids, triangles, half-circles, and quarter-circles) or three-dimensional shapes (cubes, right rectangular prisms, right circular cones, and right circular cylinders) to create a composite shape, and compose new shapes from the composite shape.

BC86ED40DFE60131784D68A86D17958E.description: Distinguish between defining attributes (e.g., triangles are closed and three-sided) versus non-defining attributes (e.g., color, orientation, overall size); build and draw shapes to possess defining attributes.

BC86ACD0DFE60131784C68A86D17958E.description: Reason with shapes and their attributes.

BC861DD0DFE60131784A68A86D17958E.description: Organize, represent, and interpret data with up to three categories; ask and answer questions about the total number of data points, how many in each category, and how many more or less are in one category than in another.

BC8598B0DFE60131784868A86D17958E.description: Tell and write time in hours and half-hours using analog and digital clocks.

comments: Limit to contexts where the object being measured is spanned by a whole number of length units with no gaps or overlaps.
BC850830DFE60131784668A86D17958E.description: Express the length of an object as a whole number of length units, by laying multiple copies of a shorter object (the length unit) end to end; understand that the length measurement of an object is the number of same-size length units that span it with no gaps or overlaps.

BC84C350DFE60131784568A86D17958E.description: Order three objects by length; compare the lengths of two objects indirectly by using a third object.

BC847430DFE60131784468A86D17958E.description: Measure lengths indirectly and by iterating length units.

BC83F220DFE60131784268A86D17958E.description: Subtract multiples of 10 in the range 10-90 from multiples of 10 in the range 10-90 (positive or zero differences), using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used.

BC83B0E0DFE60131784168A86D17958E.description: Given a two-digit number, mentally find 10 more or 10 less than the number, without having to count; explain the reasoning used.

BC836C90DFE60131784068A86D17958E.description: Add within 100, including adding a two-digit number and a one-digit number, and adding a two-digit number and a multiple of 10, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used. Understand that in adding two-digit numbers, one adds tens and tens, ones and ones; and sometimes it is necessary to compose a ten.

BC8324C0DFE60131783F68A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to add and subtract.

BC82CCE0DFE60131783E68A86D17958E.description: Compare two two-digit numbers based on meanings of the tens and ones digits, recording the results of comparisons with the symbols >, =, and <.

BC827690DFE60131783D68A86D17958E.description: The numbers 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90 refer to one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine tens (and 0 ones).

BC822FA0DFE60131783C68A86D17958E.description: The numbers from 11 to 19 are composed of a ten and one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine ones.

BC81E5E0DFE60131783B68A86D17958E.description: 10 can be thought of as a bundle of ten ones — called a "ten."

BC81A280DFE60131783A68A86D17958E.description: Understand that the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones. Understand the following as special cases:

BC8119E0DFE60131783868A86D17958E.description: Count to 120, starting at any number less than 120. In this range, read and write numerals and represent a number of objects with a written numeral.

comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.
BC808CB0DFE60131783668A86D17958E.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten

BC804B30DFE60131783568A86D17958E.description: Determine the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation relating three whole numbers.
comments: For example, determine the unknown number that makes the equation true in each of the equations 8 + ? = 11, 5 = - 3, 6 + 6 = .

BC800810DFE60131783468A86D17958E.description: Understand the meaning of the equal sign, and determine if equations involving addition and subtraction are true or false.
comments: For example, which of the following equations are true and which are false? 6 = 6, 7 = 8 - 1, 5 + 2 = 2 + 5, 4 + 1 = 5 + 2.

BC7FC0D0DFE60131783368A86D17958E.description: Work with addition and subtraction equations.

BC7F5660DFE60131783268A86D17958E.description: Add and subtract within 20, demonstrating fluency for addition and subtraction within 10. Use strategies such as counting on; making ten (e.g., 8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + 4 = 10 + 4 = 14); decomposing a number leading to a ten (e.g., 13 - 4 = 13 - 3 - 1 = 10 - 1 = 9); using the relationship between addition and subtraction (e.g., knowing that 8 + 4 = 12, one knows 12 - 8 = 4); and creating equivalent but easier or known sums (e.g., adding 6 + 7 by creating the known equivalent 6 + 6 + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13).

BC7EFB10DFE60131783168A86D17958E.description: Relate counting to addition and subtraction (e.g., by counting on 2 to add 2).

BC7E7EE0DFE60131782F68A86D17958E.description: Understand subtraction as an unknown-addend problem.
comments: For example, subtract 10 - 8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8.

BC7E3D30DFE60131782E68A86D17958E.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract.
comments: Students need not use formal terms for these properties.
To add 2 + 6 + 4, the second two numbers can be added to make a ten, so 2 + 6 + 4 = 2 + 10 = 12. (Associative property of addition.)
If 8 + 3 = 11 is known, then 3 + 8 = 11 is also known. (Commutative property of addition.)

BC7DF760DFE60131782D68A86D17958E.description: Understand and apply properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction.

BC7DB1F0DFE60131782C68A86D17958E.description: Solve word problems that call for addition of three whole numbers whose sum is less than or equal to 20, e.g., by using objects, drawings, and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

BC7D6BE0DFE60131782B68A86D17958E.description: Use addition and subtraction within 20 to solve word problems involving situations of adding to, taking from, putting together, taking apart, and comparing, with unknowns in all positions, e.g., by using objects, drawings, and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

BC7D1D70DFE60131782A68A86D17958E.description: Represent and solve problems involving addition and subtraction.

BC7C8DF0DFE60131782868A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

BC7C4190DFE60131782768A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

BC7AF7C0DFE60131782368A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.
BC7A4BA0DFE60131782168A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.

document.title: New Jersey Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

BE465630DFE601317B2768A86D17958E.description: (+) Analyze decisions and strategies using probability concepts (e.g., product testing, medical testing, pulling a hockey goalie at the end of a game).

BE45FEB0DFE601317B2668A86D17958E.description: (+) Use probabilities to make fair decisions (e.g., drawing by lots, using a random number generator).

comments: For example, compare a high-deductible versus a low-deductible automobile insurance policy using various, but reasonable, chances of having a minor or a major accident.
BE459CF0DFE601317B2568A86D17958E.description: Evaluate and compare strategies on the basis of expected values.

BE453B10DFE601317B2468A86D17958E.description: Find the expected payoff for a game of chance.
comments: For example, find the expected winnings from a state lottery ticket or a game at a fast-food restaurant.

BE44CCF0DFE601317B2368A86D17958E.description: (+) Weigh the possible outcomes of a decision by assigning probabilities to payoff values and finding expected values.

BE446160DFE601317B2268A86D17958E.description: Use probability to evaluate outcomes of decisions

comments: For example, find a current data distribution on the number of TV sets per household in the United States, and calculate the expected number of sets per household. How many TV sets would you expect to find in 100 randomly selected households?
BE440C40DFE601317B2168A86D17958E.description: (+) Develop a probability distribution for a random variable defined for a sample space in which probabilities are assigned empirically; find the expected value.

comments: For example, find the theoretical probability distribution for the number of correct answers obtained by guessing on all five questions of a multiple-choice test where each question has four choices, and find the expected grade under various grading schemes.
BE43B690DFE601317B2068A86D17958E.description: (+) Develop a probability distribution for a random variable defined for a sample space in which theoretical probabilities can be calculated; find the expected value.

BE436390DFE601317B1F68A86D17958E.description: (+) Calculate the expected value of a random variable; interpret it as the mean of the probability distribution.

BE430E10DFE601317B1E68A86D17958E.description: (+) Define a random variable for a quantity of interest by assigning a numerical value to each event in a sample space; graph the corresponding probability distribution using the same graphical displays as for data distributions.

BE42B170DFE601317B1D68A86D17958E.description: Calculate expected values and use them to solve problems

BE41F170DFE601317B1B68A86D17958E.description: (+) Use permutations and combinations to compute probabilities of compound events and solve problems.

BE419CC0DFE601317B1A68A86D17958E.description: (+) Apply the general Multiplication Rule in a uniform probability model, P(A and B) = P(A)P(B|A) = P(B)P(A|B), and interpret the answer in terms of the model.

BE4143E0DFE601317B1968A86D17958E.description: Apply the Addition Rule, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B), and interpret the answer in terms of the model.

BE40E8A0DFE601317B1868A86D17958E.description: Find the conditional probability of A given B as the fraction of B's outcomes that also belong to A, and interpret the answer in terms of the model.

BE407AE0DFE601317B1768A86D17958E.description: Use the rules of probability to compute probabilities of compound events in a uniform probability model

BE4017F0DFE601317B1668A86D17958E.description: Recognize and explain the concepts of conditional probability and independence in everyday language and everyday situations.
comments: For example, compare the chance of having lung cancer if you are a smoker with the chance of being a smoker if you have lung cancer.

BE3FBAA0DFE601317B1568A86D17958E.description: Construct and interpret two-way frequency tables of data when two categories are associated with each object being classified. Use the two-way table as a sample space to decide if events are independent and to approximate conditional probabilities.
comments: For example, collect data from a random sample of students in your school on their favorite subject among math, science, and English. Estimate the probability that a randomly selected student from your school will favor science given that the student is in tenth grade. Do the same for other subjects and compare the results.

BE3F5D00DFE601317B1468A86D17958E.description: Understand the conditional probability of A given B as P(A and B)/P(B), and interpret independence of A and B as saying that the conditional probability of A given B is the same as the probability of A, and the conditional probability of B given A is the same as the probability of B.

BE3EDB30DFE601317B1368A86D17958E.description: Understand that two events A and B are independent if the probability of A and B occurring together is the product of their probabilities, and use this characterization to determine if they are independent.

BE3E79F0DFE601317B1268A86D17958E.description: Describe events as subsets of a sample space (the set of outcomes) using characteristics (or categories) of the outcomes, or as unions, intersections, or complements of other events ("or," "and," "not").

BE3E24E0DFE601317B1168A86D17958E.description: Understand independence and conditional probability and use them to interpret data

BE3DCE00DFE601317B1068A86D17958E.description: Conditional Probability and the Rules of Probability

BE3D08D0DFE601317B0E68A86D17958E.description: Use data from a randomized experiment to compare two treatments; use simulations to decide if differences between parameters are significant.

BE3CA890DFE601317B0D68A86D17958E.description: Use data from a sample survey to estimate a population mean or proportion; develop a margin of error through the use of simulation models for random sampling.

BE3C4C50DFE601317B0C68A86D17958E.description: Recognize the purposes of and differences among sample surveys, experiments, and observational studies; explain how randomization relates to each.

BE3BE7E0DFE601317B0B68A86D17958E.description: Make inferences and justify conclusions from sample surveys, experiments, and observational studies

BE3B8570DFE601317B0A68A86D17958E.description: Decide if a specified model is consistent with results from a given data-generating process, e.g., using simulation.
comments: For example, a model says a spinning coin falls heads up with probability 0.5. Would a result of 5 tails in a row cause you to question the model?

BE3B22D0DFE601317B0968A86D17958E.description: Understand statistics as a process for making inferences about population parameters based on a random sample from that population.

BE3AAE90DFE601317B0868A86D17958E.description: Understand and evaluate random processes underlying statistical experiments

BE398DC0DFE601317B0568A86D17958E.description: Compute (using technology) and interpret the correlation coefficient of a linear fit.

BE390220DFE601317B0468A86D17958E.description: Interpret the slope (rate of change) and the intercept (constant term) of a linear model in the context of the data.

BE3842B0DFE601317B0268A86D17958E.description: Fit a linear function for a scatter plot that suggests a linear association.

BE37E930DFE601317B0168A86D17958E.description: Informally assess the fit of a function by plotting and analyzing residuals.

BE378E10DFE601317B0068A86D17958E.description: Fit a function to the data; use functions fitted to data to solve problems in the context of the data.
comments: Use given functions or choose a function suggested by the context. Emphasize linear, quadratic, and exponential models.

BE372DF0DFE601317AFF68A86D17958E.description: Represent data on two quantitative variables on a scatter plot, and describe how the variables are related.

BE36CC50DFE601317AFE68A86D17958E.description: Summarize categorical data for two categories in two-way frequency tables. Interpret relative frequencies in the context of the data (including joint, marginal, and conditional relative frequencies). Recognize possible associations and trends in the data.

BE366B30DFE601317AFD68A86D17958E.description: Summarize, represent, and interpret data on two categorical and quantitative variables

BE360160DFE601317AFC68A86D17958E.description: Use the mean and standard deviation of a data set to fit it to a normal distribution and to estimate population percentages. Recognize that there are data sets for which such a procedure is not appropriate. Use calculators, spreadsheets, and tables to estimate areas under the normal curve.

BE35A140DFE601317AFB68A86D17958E.description: Interpret differences in shape, center, and spread in the context of the data sets, accounting for possible effects of extreme data points (outliers).

BE354C20DFE601317AFA68A86D17958E.description: Use statistics appropriate to the shape of the data distribution to compare center (median, mean) and spread (interquartile range, standard deviation) of two or more different data sets.

BE34EED0DFE601317AF968A86D17958E.description: Represent data with plots on the real number line (dot plots, histograms, and box plots).

BE349890DFE601317AF868A86D17958E.description: Summarize, represent, and interpret data on a single count or measurement variable

BDAEBDF0DFE601317A1668A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.
BDAE58E0DFE601317A1568A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.

comments: Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.
BDACBCB0DFE601317A1168A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

comments: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

BDABF540DFE601317A0F68A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: New Jersey Core Curriculum Content Standards for Visual and Performing Arts

7E682D3309A64D91AA85D03FE748D2A4.description: Determine the role of art and art-making in a global society by analyzing the influence of technology on the visual, performing, and multimedia arts for consumers, creators, and performers around the world.

5E7613E1981C4FB89F9CA9558CB52AB7.description: Art and art-making reflect and affect the role of technology in a global society.

33D1EB2D9D7441C7971D96A22C42FE7D.description: Evaluate how an artist's technical proficiency may affect the creation or presentation of a work of art, as well as how the context in which a work is performed or shown may impact perceptions of its significance/meaning.

4C2609515D9E4BF4A64BE115E421BBF4.description: The cohesiveness of a work of art and its ability to communicate a theme or narrative can be directly affected by the artist's technical proficiency as well as by the manner and physical context in which it is performed or shown.

4ECB20AB35DC4739A836830A7AFDCE20.description: Formulate criteria for arts evaluation using the principles of positive critique and observation of the elements of art and principles of design, and use the criteria to evaluate works of dance, music, theatre, visual, and multimedia artwork from diverse cultural contexts and historical eras.

25835C5DD1B548AF8F8B77604FEEC777.description: Archetypal subject matter exists in all cultures and is embodied in the formal and informal aspects of art.

E313F35E8716478CB84F7A84D2BB68CF.description: Evaluate how exposure to various cultures influences individual, emotional, intellectual, and kinesthetic responses to artwork.

55CF531B47BA4254872F37A7715019CF.description: Criteria for assessing the historical significance, craftsmanship, cultural context, and originality of art are often expressed in qualitative, discipline-specific arts terminology.

E89E08DC516047DA8553BBA27DAF0CE4.description: Develop informed personal responses to an assortment of artworks across the four arts disciplines (dance, music, theatre, and visual art), using historical significance, craftsmanship, cultural context, and originality as criteria for assigning value to the works.

1AFD1332DBE448C2BFEC5C73E4E93096.description: Artistic styles, trends, movements, and historical responses to various genres of art evolve over time.

3DDFF89154074DD0933F43B98972384C.description: Speculate on the artist's intent, using discipline-specific arts terminology and citing embedded clues to substantiate the hypothesis.

33BF9ED2B99A4BC8ACB3D73C6C963D71.description: Contextual clues within artworks often reveal artistic intent, enabling the viewer to hypothesize the artist's concept.

5C61FD30B36A4BD3B7EF4DABE60EEEA1.description: Use contextual clues to differentiate between unique and common properties and to discern the cultural implications of works of dance, music, theatre, and visual art.

C93E382152EB4EB29DC7C91597C27528.description: Recognition of fundamental elements within various arts disciplines (dance, music, theatre, and visual art) is dependent on the ability to decipher cultural implications embedded in artworks.

E19F727079194E15A3AA8A241B2689C1.description: Aesthetic Responses & Critique Methodologies: All students will demonstrate and apply an understanding of arts philosophies, judgment, and analysis to works of art in dance, music, theatre, and visual art.

34F50CCB3D0343A08480A8BD6ABB44AD.description: Identify the styles and artistic processes used in the creation of culturally and historically diverse two- and three-dimensional artworks, and emulate those styles by creating an original body of work.

D5ECCCEC93C64C1F9F8DEB97D31237D4.description: Two- and three-dimensional artworks can be rendered culturally specific by using the tools, techniques, styles, materials, and methodologies that are germane to a particular cultural style.

AE74CC90ACC1422898FFB1DEEE92B81C.description: Analyze the syntax and compositional and stylistic principles of two- and three-dimensional artworks in multiple art media (including computer-assisted artwork), and interpret themes and symbols suggested by the artworks.

C6DA0CC12E0B4A89B56DF2BD873DF7A4.description: Artists interpret/render themes using traditional art media and methodologies as well as new art media and methodologies.

F013551494D74438A7058A0C418EC7F0.description: Organize an exhibit of personal works of visual art that convey a high level of understanding of how the expression of ideas relates to the art media, art mediums, and techniques used.

B47434FBED7F4960A22F6706FB64A380.description: The artist's understanding of the relationships among art media, methodology, and visual statement allows the artist to use expressionism, abstractionism (nonobjective art), realism/naturalism, impressionism, and other genre styles to convey ideas to an audience.

031BABD248DC432B986F0D8936244319.description: Produce an original body of artwork in one or more art mediums that demonstrates mastery of visual literacy, methods, techniques, and cultural understanding.

DBC229696EEA41BB9BFA3153614E427E.description: Culturally and historically diverse art media, art mediums, techniques, and styles impact originality and interpretation of the artistic statement.

EA31EFCDEFC842A4B18F70E4366734F0.description: Synthesize the elements of art and principles of design in an original portfolio of two- and three-dimensional artworks that reflects personal style and a high degree of technical proficiency and expressivity.

2FF9812B5CA54CBDB7558985884BDB27.description: How individuals manipulate the elements of art and principles of design results in original portfolios that reflect choice and personal stylistic nuance.

2B742D969BF34DB8BF6200E84ABA8892.description: Create and evaluate performances by citing evidence of specific physical choices, sustained vocal technique, and clearly motivated actions.

680A0DE108244EC3BAB589E1B6CEC854.description: Presentation of believable, multidimensional characters in scripted and improvised performances requires application of specific physical choices, sustained vocal technique, and clearly motivated actions.

DF8F7357D0764EC9942A10893D8A03B2.description: Create plays that include well-structured plots and subplots, clear thematic intent, original characters, and technical theatrical elements appropriate to a variety of theatrical genres.

143A1160F23344AE876886599F26AC03.description: Effective scripted and improvisational performances require informed, supported, and sustained choices by actors, directors, and designers. Theatre genres are created by combining complex narrative structures, technical theatrical elements, and thematic intent.

E4225004DD9542E8A923BB40789ED6D0.description: Arrange simple pieces for voice or instrument using a variety of traditional and nontraditional sound sources or electronic media, and/or analyze prepared scores using music composition software.

6BA4F1D222FC4000A8562D9190246913.description: Basic vocal and instrumental arranging skills require theoretical understanding of music composition.

47583892579547EF8F3842C8889CE784.description: Improvise works through the conscious manipulation of the elements of music, using a variety of traditional and nontraditional sound sources, including electronic sound-generating equipment and music generation programs.

B1F42A0CA00F4716AACC0F783A173617.description: Understanding of how to manipulate the elements of music is a contributing factor to musical artistry.

E090EDA64C3A4672B7E5EDCB49ACF7DF.description: Analyze how the elements of music are manipulated in original or prepared musical scores.

80A71C6154C4495C8388DB294598BD72.description: The ability to read and interpret music impacts musical fluency.

62DAA9DCF50A453E8A705CFD0871FB2E.description: Analyze compositions from different world cultures and genres with respect to technique, musicality, and stylistic nuance, and/or perform excerpts with technical accuracy, appropriate musicality, and the relevant stylistic nuance.

DB492AFC1A114280A569784CE5059F08.description: Technical accuracy, musicality, and stylistic considerations vary according to genre, culture, and historical era.

7A4E9016CD384395A433AA01511F4ECD.description: Collaborate in the design and production of dances that use choreographic structures and incorporate various media and/or technologies.

A86FA799C6E14C4D8602C27D83BB8F9C.description: Dance production is collaborative and requires choreographic, technological, design, and performance skill.

92DB73122ADD46B7B15816E242F863CD.description: Demonstrate dance artistry with technical proficiency, musicality, stylistic nuance, clarity of choreographic intent, and efficiency of movement through the application of proper body mechanics.

C47237E6427E4345ACA4B6D631799627.description: Dance artistry is achieved through refined technique, musicality, clarity of choreographic intent, stylistic nuance, and application of proper body mechanics.

E6836E0598544015953161ABA4CBD811.description: Create theme-based solo and ensemble dances that have unity of form and content, conceptual coherence, and aesthetic unity.

E752E1168C9E41B6950AC11D046E307E.description: Aesthetic quality results from conceptual coherence and from understanding and application of the principle unity of form and content.

039EF961B1FC4B8691719A5C9498759D.description: Integrate and recombine movement vocabulary drawn from a variety of dance genres, using improvisation as a choreographic tool to create solo and ensemble compositions.

1F9371C16B7E454C972785402428AFD2.description: Creating highly integrated improvisational movement sequences develops personal style for solo and ensemble work. Characteristics of style vary broadly across dance genres.

A0E20304DBAB40BA8D59F3C437350D7A.description: Performance: All students will synthesize those skills, media, methods, and technologies appropriate to creating, performing, and/or presenting works of art in dance, music, theatre, and visual art.

12D11CD363E64C41973F132744148E4E.description: Justify the impact of innovations in the arts (e.g., the availability of music online) on societal norms and habits of mind in various historical eras.

D8147066E0A94B36A1F3785CA0DA8955.description: Access to the arts has a positive influence on the quality of an individual's lifelong learning, personal expression, and contributions to community and global citizenship.

976E1B75B4424B00B5C77909894A7AD5.description: Determine how dance, music, theatre, and visual art have influenced world cultures throughout history.

5A8F4D974A8E45B3B372A8196E282033.description: Cultural and historical events impact art-making as well as how audiences respond to works of art.

A2C8EB7962874FB58E1D90ABEE6F98BE.description: History of the Arts and Culture

58F970FD1A8D44A8A0F9EF6E908E01F6.description: History of the Arts and Culture: All students will understand the role, development, and influence of the arts throughout history and across cultures.

222A6276FBBD42AA83FCAA64BFD85E7E.description: Translate literary, musical, theatrical, and dance compositions by using them as stimulus/inspiration for corresponding visual artworks.

EA0A598123E14976827E52B13A10E720.description: Stimuli for the creation of artworks can come from many places, including other arts disciplines.

DF724D2EED204991A3BB2C8A4B0F1440.description: Distinguish innovative applications of the elements of art and principles of design in visual artworks from diverse cultural perspectives and identify specific cross-cultural themes.

51FC01C9649F4662B914B7D1CDDDBA53.description: Common themes exist in artwork from a variety of cultures across time and are communicated through metaphor, symbolism, and allegory.

1022051B6F4C4427889FA95CB8C772AE.description: Apply the basic physical and chemical properties (e.g., light, electricity, color, paint, scenic construction, costumes, makeup, and audio components) inherent in technical theatre to safely implement theatre design.

A78023571CA54FDAB0436A62802FDD99.description: Theatre production is an art, but it is also a science requiring knowledge of safety procedures, materials, technology, and construction techniques.

8BE1993BDE6243F791F2FA14C7228092.description: Formulate a process of script analysis to identify how the physical, emotional, and social dimensions of a character are communicated through the application of acting techniques.

C8B4713B750B43CABD7796A35BC847F1.description: Characters have physical, emotional, and social dimensions that can be communicated through the application of acting techniques.

1F1B02B514D74078B35C9903033CE5DE.description: Analyze examples of theatre's influence on history and history's influence on theatre in Western and non-Western theatre traditions.

C0F180FBA1D5463EBE0ED9B1E2C8CA8B.description: Theatre and the arts play a significant role in human history and culture.

E2D2BA809D7C4FC2B4807C12975A5FAF.description: Synthesize knowledge of the elements of music in the deconstruction and performance of complex musical scores from diverse cultural contexts.

B3471E4A418D4A37A9E7E388AE145922.description: Musical proficiency is characterized by the ability to sight-read advanced notation. Musical fluency is also characterized by the ability to classify and replicate the stylistic differences in music of varying traditions.

75EB10AE399548028BE8F8150AE07C1B.description: Examine how aspects of meter, rhythm, tonality, intervals, chords, and harmonic progressions are organized and manipulated to establish unity and variety in genres of musical compositions.

D5E9151338054A4D9D5984D880A3283E.description: Understanding nuanced stylistic differences among various genres of music is a component of musical fluency. Meter, rhythm, tonality, and harmonics are determining factors in the categorization of musical genres.

5E1C3E3FC8CD4653B9C25742A263DAD8.description: Synthesize knowledge of anatomical principles related to body alignment, body patterning, balance, strength, and coordination in compositions and performances.

514E303D3FA247BD9A38BC286D600E36.description: Artistry in dance performance is accomplished through complete integration of anatomical principles and clear direction of intent and purpose.

A6324409C953421D88D25D3FD1FE84A0.description: Analyze issues of gender, ethnicity, socio-economic status, politics, age, and physical conditioning in relation to dance performances.

3B55CB4867574EC180C2709C1527EAFB.description: Interpretation of dance is heavily reliant on its context.

F2477157094C4CBFBCB6A891C56B7279.description: Categorize the elements, principles, and choreographic structures of dance masterworks.

7A227315006041D9B7E26E554AE57086.description: Acute kinesthetic awareness and mastery of composition are essential for creating and interpreting master works of art.

3B8EA7DCCD654D62A4A0D00171A1F0C1.description: Articulate understanding of choreographic structures or forms (e.g., palindrome, theme and variation, rondo, retrograde, inversion, narrative, and accumulation) in master works of dance.

A0C617D83D8D40F1A31814BC4E8B3DBA.description: Creating master works in dance requires ability to comprehend, articulate, and manipulate time, space, and energy across and within a broad spectrum of choreographic structures and through the use of many choreographic devices.

1677648AE47C4CBF88CF6A825F06FFF9.description: Use appropriate terms in conversation (e.g., programming, language, data, RAM, ROM, Boolean logic terms).

4E2C65A2213C43998035DC85D3B1A663.description: Demonstrate an understanding of the relationship between hardware and software.

8FE6224E712945558D2F7376D8D2B7DA.description: Identify ways computers are used that have had an impact across the range of human activity and within different careers where they are used.

85FB961931D1451DB980438254946BF3.description: Computational thinking and computer programming as tools used in design and engineering.

E676632B316E4694BCF0BD35E8DFA8A7.description: Computational Thinking: Programming: Computational thinking builds and enhances problem solving, allowing students to move beyond using knowledge to creating knowledge.

AD19FEC4722040C7B4B39D38918D035E.description: Identify and explain how the resources and processes used in the production of a current technological product can be modified to have a more positive impact on the environment.

876FC61809254D3D93984C12D191FC66.description: Explain the impact of resource selection and the production process in the development of a common or technological product or system.

A85A434ACBB14117BEAE1C7924F9F50C.description: Assess the impact of products and systems.

2D6BAD880D4F40EEB943EA2EAF961AC8.description: Identify the design constraints and trade-offs involved in designing a prototype (e.g., how the prototype might fail and how it might be improved) by completing a design problem and reporting results in a multimedia presentation, design portfolio or engineering notebook.

F1873B546B3543A8B860A2BC0534B87E.description: Abilities for a Technological World: The designed world is the product of a design process that provides the means to convert resources into products and systems.

B4090EBAC2E84DA3B7A737AC3D389BE4.description: Develop a proposal for a chosen solution that include models (physical, graphical or mathematical) to communicate the solution to peers.

763280DAB84C44518416F065AEE165A2.description: Collaborate with peers and experts in the field to research and develop a product using the design process, data analysis and trends, and maintain a design log with annotated sketches to record the developmental cycle.

91CFA89C204641D687A1BD4C3D0F203E.description: Collaborate to examine a malfunctioning system and identify the step-by-step process used to troubleshoot, evaluate and test options to repair the product, presenting the better solution.

A205F490130640C29FCA97331D6F66E7.description: The role of troubleshooting, research and development, invention and innovation and experimentation in problem solving.

D2FC3F23B5314210B0E3F91D6E1AADB0.description: Explain the interdependence of a subsystem that operates as part of a system. Create a technical sketch of a product with materials and measurements labeled.

EFA4CD5CE34F4CA39051BBF8E28372D7.description: Identify the steps in the design process that would be used to solve a designated problem.

F60CE565684A4699B93CF6675A947D13.description: Examine a system, consider how each part relates to other parts, and discuss a part to redesign to improve the system.

04E28E27CD4749C1B53513594A609493.description: Research a product that was designed for a specific demand and identify how the product has changed to meet new demands (i.e. telephone for communication - smart phone for mobility needs).

D358DB1206074A3CB6CB349A50BEFA1A.description: The Nature of Technology: Creativity and Innovation Technology systems impact every aspect of the world in which we live.

4C32C565794F40BE8DF3673925D25B82.description: Creativity and Innovation: Students demonstrate creative thinking, construct knowledge and develop innovative products and process using technology.
